title: Independent Sets in Multiset Profile Graphs via Weighted Local Covers — conjecture conj:prime-checksum-optimality
open: For every prime $q$, does there exist an integer $d_0(q)$ such that the conjectured prime-checksum optimality holds for all dimensions $d \ge d_0(q)$? Formally, the conjecture asks that such a threshold $d_0(q)$ exists for each prime $q$.
solved_when: For every prime $q$, an explicit integer $d_0(q)$ is exhibited such that the prime-checksum optimality conjecture is proven for all cases at and beyond that threshold.
why: The conjecture underpins the claimed optimal behavior of prime checksums in the multiset-profile setting; establishing the threshold settles when the optimality is guaranteed to hold.

title: The exact total degree threshold for the square of a Hamilton cycle in
open: For every $k \ge 2$, does there exist an $l_0 = l_0(k)$ such that, for every $l \ge l_0$ and every $n = lm$, each $n$-vertex digraph $D$ satisfying $\delta(D) \ge \frac{2(k+2)}{k+3}n$ contains a $C_l^k$-factor?
solved_when: For every $k \ge 2$, an $l_0(k)$ is exhibited such that every $n$-vertex digraph with $n = lm$ for some $l \ge l_0$ and minimum total degree at least $\frac{2(k+2)}{k+3}n$ contains a $C_l^k$-factor, or a counterexample refuting the statement for some $k$.
why: It would pin down the exact total degree threshold forcing a perfect tiling by powers of directed cycles, a natural directed analogue of the Pósa–Seymour-type packing question.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13831v2 (Zhilan Wang, Shuo Wei, Jin Yan)

title: Feedback vertex sets in oriented graphs — conjecture conj:NL
open: Can every planar oriented graph have its vertex set partitioned into two parts, each of which induces an acyclic subgraph? Equivalently, is the vertex set of every planar oriented graph the union of two acyclic sets?
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with a counterexample) is given that every planar oriented graph admits a vertex-partition into two acyclic induced subgraphs.
why: It would resolve the natural directed analogue of partitioning planar graphs into independent or bounded-mess parts, clarifying how orientation and acyclicity interact under planarity.

title: The Lean Number of a Hypergraph
open: Which hypergraphs achieve a given lean number? A construction in the source paper shows the lower bound of the edge-count lemma is tight for a whole family of hypergraphs, so we ask: can we characterize the collection of hypergraphs for which $\ell(H) = k$?
solved_when: A complete characterization (structural, algorithmic, or extremal) of the hypergraphs $H$ with $\ell(H) = k$ is given, for each $k$, matching the tight instances from the source paper.
why: The tightness examples show the current bound cannot be improved in general; a characterization would identify exactly which hypergraphs are extremal and delimit when the bound is loose.

title: The Lean Number of a Hypergraph
open: Do infinitely many knots or links have lean number 5, and do any knots or links attain lean number 6 or arbitrarily large lean numbers? In particular, while a lean number of 5 appears rare among knots but frequent among links, it is unknown whether the invariant is unbounded over all knots and links.
solved_when: Either an infinite family of knots or links with lean number 5 is exhibited, or examples with lean number 6 (or arbitrarily large lean number) are produced; conversely, a proof that only finitely many exist or that the lean number is bounded would settle the corresponding part.
why: It would clarify whether the lean number behaves as an unbounded knot invariant or collapses to small values, explaining the observed scarcity of lean number 5 among knots versus links.

title: Three-Bit Flows and Cycle Covers. Part I — conjecture conj:cdc
open: Does every finite bridgeless multigraph admit a cycle double cover? That is, can the edges of such a graph each be covered exactly twice by a collection of cycles?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14140v1 (Shiva Kintali).
solved_when: A proof, or a counterexample, is given for the assertion that every finite bridgeless multigraph has a family of cycles covering each edge exactly twice.
why: The cycle double cover conjecture is a central structural question about how bridgeless graphs decompose into cycles; resolving it would settle a long-standing obstruction in graph decomposition theory.

title: Semi-Streaming Matching in a Single Pass I: A New Framework for Lower
open: What is the best approximation ratio a single-pass semi-streaming algorithm can achieve for maximum matching? More precisely, determine the optimal trade-off between approximation guarantee and space (near-linear in the number of edges) for one-pass algorithms in this model.
status: The question is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.14644v1 (Sepehr Assadi, Max Jiang, Mars Xiang); no resolution is recorded in the census.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds are established for the approximation ratio of single-pass semi-streaming maximum matching, pinning down the optimal constant achievable within the semi-streaming space budget.
why: It identifies the exact limit of one-pass graph streaming for one of the model's flagship problems, separating what randomness and space can and cannot accomplish in a single pass.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14644v1 (Sepehr Assadi, Max Jiang, Mars Xiang)

title: Semi-Streaming Matching in a Single Pass I: A New Framework for Lower
open: Is a 0.5-approximation truly the best possible for the semi-streaming matching problem? More formally, does every single-pass semi-streaming algorithm for maximum matching admit an instance on which it achieves an approximation ratio no better than 0.5?
solved_when: Either a semi-streaming matching algorithm is exhibited whose approximation ratio strictly exceeds 0.5 on every instance, or it is proved that no such algorithm can beat the 0.5 barrier.
why: The 0.5 barrier is the long-standing default guarantee in semi-streaming matching; breaking it in either direction would fundamentally revise our understanding of what one pass over an edge stream suffices to compute.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14644v1 (Sepehr Assadi, Max Jiang, Mars Xiang)

title: Semi-Streaming Matching in a Single Pass II: Greedy is Optimal
open: Can any single-pass semi-streaming algorithm for maximum matching achieve an approximation factor strictly better than the half-approximation guaranteed by the greedy algorithm? Formally, is there a trade-off breaking this barrier in the vertex-arrival semi-streaming model?
status: The question of improving the greedy algorithm's half-approximation is stated as open in the source paper (2026), "Semi-Streaming Matching in a Single Pass II: Greedy is Optimal" (Sepehr Assadi, Max Jiang, Mars Xiang), http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14656v2, from which it is extracted as a curated open problem.
solved_when: A single-pass semi-streaming algorithm (or a proof that none exists) settles whether the half-approximation of greedy can be improved upon; no quantitative target beyond the half-approximation barrier is stated in the record.
why: The greedy half-approximation has been the standing benchmark since the model's introduction; improving it would advance the basic frontier of streaming graph algorithms, while a lower bound would establish greedy's optimality.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14656v2 (Sepehr Assadi, Max Jiang, Mars Xiang)

title: Beneš and Shuffle-Exchange Counterexamples
open: Does external connectivity suffice for rearrangeability in the Beneš setting? Formally, in the Open Problem Garden graph formulation of the Beneš conjecture: for a simple regular ordered two-stage graph, does external connectivity imply rearrangeability?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given showing that external connectivity implies rearrangeability (or fails to) for every simple regular ordered two-stage graph in the formulation above.
why: It would settle a long-standing conjecture about when two-stage switching networks can realize all connection patterns, resolving a basic structural question in the theory of rearrangeable networks.

title: Beneš and Shuffle-Exchange Counterexamples
open: Does external connectivity of a graph force rearrangeability? Concretely, for simple regular ordered two-stage graphs, the question is whether external connectivity implies rearrangeability, as formulated on the Open Problem Garden graph page for these Beneš and shuffle-exchange counterexample problems.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), extracted from a curated open-problems paper; the Open Problem Garden pages record the partition and graph formulations as open, with the graph page formulating the question as whether external connectivity forces rearrangeability for simple regular ordered two-stage graphs. Key work: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15296v1 (Przemek Chojecki).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given of whether external connectivity forces rearrangeability for simple regular ordered two-stage graphs, settling both the partition and graph formulations as stated on the Open Problem Garden pages.
why: These Beneš and shuffle-exchange counterexamples sit at the boundary between externally connected and rearrangeable networks, so resolving the implication would pin down exactly when connectivity suffices for rearrangeability in two-stage switching constructions.

title: NP-Hardness of Connected Components Reconfiguration under Component Ju
open: Is it NP-hard to decide reconfigurability of connected components (e.g., under component-jump-style moves) on chordal graphs when the multiset of component sizes is constrained? Settling this would resolve the open problem posed by Nakahata on chordal graphs under multiset size constraints.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of NP-hardness for the reconfiguration problem on chordal graphs under multiset size constraints is established, thereby resolving Nakahata's open problem.
why: It extends the hardness landscape of graph reconfiguration from general graphs to the structured class of chordal graphs, closing an explicitly posed gap in the literature.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15737v1 (Naoki Kitamura, Seitaro Kawaguchi, Yuya Terashima)

title: NP-Hardness of Connected Components Reconfiguration under Component Ju
open: Is Connected Components Reconfiguration under the component-jump rule NP-hard on chordal graphs when a multiset size constraint is imposed? Formally, since caterpillar graphs are a subclass of chordal graphs, does the existing NP-hardness for caterpillars immediately imply NP-hardness for chordal graphs under this constraint, thereby resolving Nakahata's open problem on chordal graphs under multiset size constraints?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.15737v1 (Naoki Kitamura, Seitaro Kawaguchi, Yuya Terashima). The observation that caterpillar graphs are a subclass of chordal graphs suggests the caterpillar NP-hardness result may carry over to chordal graphs under the multiset size constraint.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of NP-hardness of Connected Components Reconfiguration under component jump on chordal graphs subject to a multiset size constraint is established, resolving Nakahata's open problem.
why: It would settle a stated open problem on the complexity landscape of token-reconfiguration problems restricted to chordal graphs, completing the classification begun by the caterpillar case.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15737v1 (Naoki Kitamura, Seitaro Kawaguchi, Yuya Terashima)

title: NP-Hardness of Connected Components Reconfiguration under Component Ju
open: Is the Connected Components Reconfiguration (CCR) problem tractable when the number of connected components is bounded by a constant? More precisely, Nakahata asked whether CCR becomes tractable under such a bound, and the question is whether this holds or a negative (NP-hardness) answer can be established.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.15737v1 (Naoki Kitamura, Seitaro Kawaguchi, Yuya Terashima), which gives a negative answer to a different open problem of Nakahata concerning whether CCR becomes tractable when the number of connected components is bounded by a constant.
solved_when: A proof (algorithmic or hardness) resolves whether CCR with a constant bound on the number of connected components is tractable — either a polynomial-time algorithm in that regime, or a proof of NP-hardness.
why: It settles whether the number of connected components is the right structural parameter governing the complexity of CCR, separating the tractable and hard regimes of reconfiguration.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15737v1 (Naoki Kitamura, Seitaro Kawaguchi, Yuya Terashima)

title: A proof of the cycle double cover conjecture by OpenAI: An exposition — conjecture conj:small-cdc
open: Does every simple 2-edge-connected graph admit a cycle double cover — a collection of cycles such that each edge appears in exactly two of them? Formally, is it true for every simple $2$-edge-connected graph on $n$ vertices?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), an exposition by Sang-il Oum, available at http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16356v3.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every simple $2$-edge-connected graph has a family of cycles covering each edge exactly twice, or an explicit counterexample.
why: The cycle double cover conjecture is a central structural question about how edge connectivity forces a cycle decomposition; a resolution settles a long-standing problem in graph theory.

title: A proof of the cycle double cover conjecture by OpenAI: An exposition — conjecture conj:strong
open: Does every $2$-connected graph admit a strong embedding on a surface — that is, an embedding in which each face is bounded by a cycle? A positive answer would yield the strong form of the cycle double cover conjecture for this class of graphs.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16356v3 (Sang-il Oum).
solved_when: A proof, or a counterexample, is given for the statement that every $2$-connected graph has a strong embedding on some surface.
why: A strong embedding implies that each edge lies on the boundary of exactly two faces bounded by cycles, directly producing a cycle double cover; it is the strongest embedding-theoretic route to the conjecture.

title: A proof of the cycle double cover conjecture by OpenAI: An exposition — conjecture conj:5-cdc
open: Does every bridgeless graph admit a cycle double cover using at most 5 cycles? Formally, is it true that every bridgeless graph has a 5-cycle double cover?
solved_when: A proof, or disproof, that every bridgeless graph has a family of at most 5 cycles covering each edge exactly twice.
why: The cycle double cover conjecture is a central open problem in structural graph theory; resolving the 5-cycle variant would settle the strongest natural form of the conjecture.

title: A proof of the cycle double cover conjecture by OpenAI: An exposition
open: Does every bridgeless graph admit an orientable $5$-cycle double cover? That is, can the edges of any bridgeless graph each be covered exactly twice by a family of at most five cycles whose incidence structure is orientable?
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper (2026), available at http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16356v3 (Sang-il Oum).
solved_when: A proof, for every bridgeless graph, of the existence of an orientable cycle double cover using at most $5$ cycles.
why: Resolving it settles the quantitative form of the cycle double cover conjecture with the smallest proposed constant, tightening the classical demand for some finite cover to a bound of five.

title: A proof of the cycle double cover conjecture by OpenAI: An exposition — conjecture con:5cdc-matroid

why: It is a matroidal form of the cycle double cover conjecture, so a proof would extend that classical circle of ideas beyond graphs; the record gives no further consequence.

title: Supersaturation in Nosal graphs: Triangles and books — problem prob-bk-13
open: Does every $m$-edge Nosal graph contain a book of size $\frac{1}{3}m$? More precisely, is there always a collection of triangles sharing a common edge of size at least one third of the number of edges?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.16746v1 (Hongzhang Chen, Yongtao Li, Quanyu Tang).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via counterexample) that every $m$-edge Nosal graph has a book of size $\frac{1}{3}m$.
why: It would settle a concrete supersaturation question for triangle-rich (Nosal) graphs, sharpening how triangles in such graphs must concentrate into books rather than scatter.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16746v1 (Hongzhang Chen, Yongtao Li, Quanyu Tang)

title: Highly connected spanning oriented subdigraphs in generalizations of s — conjecture conj:kstrongorG
open: Is there an integer function $g(k)$ such that every $g(k)$-connected graph admits a $k$-strong orientation? Equivalently, can sufficiently high vertex-connectivity alone guarantee a highly arc-strong spanning oriented subdigraph?
solved_when: An explicit integer function $g(k)$ is exhibited, with proof that every $g(k)$-connected graph has a $k$-strong orientation.
why: It would establish that vertex-connectivity of an undirected graph is enough to force highly strong orientations, giving a clean quantitative bridge between graph connectivity and orientation strength.

title: Highly connected spanning oriented subdigraphs in generalizations of s — conjecture conj1
open: Does every $2k$-strong digraph contain a spanning $k$-strong oriented graph? Formally, is the Jackson–Thomassen conjecture true: every $2k$-strong digraph admits a spanning oriented subgraph that remains $k$-strong?
status: The conjecture is attributed to Jackson and Thomassen and is stated as open in the source paper (2026); see http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17150v2 (Jia Zhou, Jørgen Bang-Jensen, Tong Zhou).
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the statement that every $2k$-strong digraph contains a spanning $k$-strong oriented graph.
why: It would show that high strong connectivity in digraphs can always be realized by an oriented graph, tightening the link between strong connectivity and orientation structure.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17150v2 (Jia Zhou, Jørgen Bang-Jensen, Tong Zhou)

title: Highly connected spanning oriented subdigraphs in generalizations of s — conjecture conj2
open: Does there exist a function $f(k)$ so that every $f(k)$-strong digraph on at least $2k+1$ vertices contains a spanning $k$-strong oriented graph?
solved_when: Explicit functions $f(k)$ are given, or existence is proven, such that every $f(k)$-strong digraph on at least $2k+1$ vertices has a spanning $k$-strong oriented subgraph; equivalently, a construction of such an $f$ for all $k$.
why: It would establish that high vertex-connectivity in digraphs guarantees highly connected spanning orientations, a structural foundation for decomposition and orientation questions in directed graph theory.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17150v2 (Jia Zhou, Jørgen Bang-Jensen, Tong Zhou)

title: Highly connected spanning oriented subdigraphs in generalizations of s — conjecture conj:SDcase
open: Does every $(2k-1)$-strong semicomplete digraph on at least $2k+1$ vertices contain a spanning $k$-strong tournament? In other words, can such a digraph always be thinned to a spanning tournament while retaining half (rounded down) of its vertex-connectivity?
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.17150v2 (Jia Zhou, Jørgen Bang-Jensen, Tong Zhou); no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or a counterexample) of the statement that every $(2k-1)$-strong semicomplete digraph on at least $2k+1$ vertices contains a spanning $k$-strong tournament, for all $k$.
why: It would show that high vertex-connectivity in semicomplete digraphs can always be realized by a spanning tournament, a minimal sparse substructure, strengthening our understanding of how connectivity behaves under sparsification.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17150v2 (Jia Zhou, Jørgen Bang-Jensen, Tong Zhou)

title: A note on tree-cycle Ramsey numbers
open: Is the Ramsey number of any $n$-vertex tree against a cycle of odd length $m$ (with $m \geq 5$ and $n \geq (2m-1)/3$) exactly $2n-1$? Formally, does $R(T_{n},C_{m})=2n-1$ hold throughout this range of parameters?
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper, arXiv:2607.17831v1 (Ting Huang, Yanbo Zhang, Yaojun Chen), posted 2026; no resolution is recorded in the census.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $R(T_{n},C_{m})=2n-1$ for all odd $m \geq 5$ and all $n \geq (2m-1)/3$, where $T_{n}$ is any tree on $n$ vertices.
why: Settling this would give the exact value of the tree-cycle Ramsey number in a broad range of parameters, completing a natural chapter of generalized Ramsey theory in which cycles are paired with trees rather than complete graphs.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17831v1 (Ting Huang, Yanbo Zhang, Yaojun Chen)

title: Frustration index of a signed planar graph and the feedback vertex set — conjecture conj:bipartite
open: Does every bipartite planar graph have a feedback vertex set of size at most $\frac{3v(G)}{8}$? That is, is $\mathrm{fvs}(G) \le \frac{3v(G)}{8}$ for all bipartite planar $G$?
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every bipartite planar graph $G$ satisfies $\mathrm{fvs}(G) \le \frac{3v(G)}{8}$, where $v(G)$ is the number of vertices.
why: It would pin down the worst-case size of a feedback vertex set — equivalently, the frustration index — for signed bipartite planar graphs, a natural structural bound between planarity and bipartiteness.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17983v1 (Sirui Chen, Jiaao Li, Zhouningxin Wang)

title: Towards a strengthening of the second neighborhood conjecture — conjecture conj:SMC
open: Does every oriented graph contain a strong Seymour vertex — a vertex whose second out-neighborhood is at least as large as its first? The conjecture conj:SMC strengthens Seymour's second neighborhood conjecture.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that every oriented graph contains a strong Seymour vertex is given, as measured against conjecture conj:SMC as stated in the source paper.
why: It strengthens the classical second neighborhood conjecture, so a proof resolves a harder variant of a central problem on oriented graphs, while a counterexample delimits how far Seymour's conjecture can be pushed.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18047v2 (Yandong Bai, Binlong Li, Boram Park)

title: Towards a strengthening of the second neighborhood conjecture — conjecture conj:SSNC
open: Does every oriented graph contain a Seymour vertex — a vertex whose second out-neighborhood is at least as large as its first? In the language of the source, this asks whether a strengthening of the Second Neighborhood Conjecture (conjecture conj:SSNC) holds for all oriented graphs.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that every oriented graph contains a Seymour vertex, as conjectured by conj:SSNC.
why: It would establish a stronger form of Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture, extending a central extremal question about digraph neighborhoods; a counterexample would sharply delimit where the conjecture can hold.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18047v2 (Yandong Bai, Binlong Li, Boram Park)

title: Towards a strengthening of the second neighborhood conjecture — conjecture conj:SMCinT
open: Does every tournament contain a strong Seymour vertex? That is, a vertex whose second out-neighborhood is at least as large as its first out-neighborhood in the strong sense asserted by conjecture conj:SMCinT, a strengthening of the classical second neighborhood conjecture for tournaments.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) of the statement that every tournament contains a strong Seymour vertex is given, as formulated in conjecture conj:SMCinT.
why: It would strengthen the classical second neighborhood conjecture within tournaments, extending a basic structural guarantee about out-neighborhoods in oriented complete graphs.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18047v2 (Yandong Bai, Binlong Li, Boram Park)

title: Acyclic Poset Multiplihedra and their Quotients
open: Are the three natural equivalence relations on colored pipings of a poset $P$ — generated respectively by adding blue pipes, by adding red pipes, and by both additions together — realized as polytopes obtained by collapsing faces of the acyclic multiplihedron, with the third, combined relation yielding the interval polytope of the order polytope of $P$?
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.18651v2 (Stefan Forcey, Ross Glew, Christopher Tapo).
solved_when: It is shown (or refuted) that the quotient posets arising from the three equivalence relations on colored pipings of a poset $P$ are realized via face collapses of the acyclic multiplihedron, and that in the case where both the blue-pipe and red-pipe additions are imposed, the resulting polytope is the interval polytope of the order polytope of $P$.
why: It would connect the combinatorics of colored pipings on posets to concrete polytopal geometry of the acyclic multiplihedron, identifying the combined quotient with the well-studied interval polytope of the order polytope.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18651v2 (Stefan Forcey, Ross Glew, Christopher Tapo)

why: The problem is extracted from a curated open-problems paper; resolving it would settle the stated conjecture about stretched Schubert structure constants and key coefficients.

title: On the autotopism groups and the equivalence of finite cyclic semifiel
open: Can cyclic semifields be completely classified up to isotopy, with their autotopism groups fully determined — thereby closing the remaining cases left open by Dempwolff?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), available at http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19172v1 (Paolo Santonastaso, Yue Zhou).
solved_when: A complete classification of cyclic semifields up to isotopy exists, together with the full determination of their autotopism groups, covering the cases left open by Dempwolff.
why: It settles the outstanding cases of Dempwolff's classification problem for cyclic semifields, giving a full picture of when such semifields are isotopic and how their autotopism groups behave.

title: On the autotopism groups and the equivalence of finite cyclic semifiel
open: Are the rank-metric codes associated with cyclic semifields — equivalently, cyclic skew-polynomial MRD codes — distinguishable by their equivalence structure, as Sheekey asked? Formally, this asks for a complete classification of cyclic semifields up to isotopy, together with the classification of the associated cyclic skew-polynomial MRD codes up to linear and semilinear equivalence.
status: The question was stated as open in the source paper (2026), in a curated open-problems context; the record gives no prior partial results. Key work: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19172v1 (Paolo Santonastaso, Yue Zhou).
solved_when: A complete classification of cyclic semifields up to isotopy is given, and in parallel the associated cyclic skew-polynomial MRD codes are classified up to linear and semilinear equivalence.
why: The classification settles Sheekey's open question on the equivalence of these rank-metric codes and resolves two long-standing open problems in the area, determining exactly when two such codes or semifields are the same object in disguise.

title: On the autotopism groups and the equivalence of finite cyclic semifiel
open: Can the autotopism groups of finite cyclic semifields be completely determined, and can the isotopy (equivalence) problem for this family be fully resolved? In formal terms, the goal is a complete description of Aut(S) for every cyclic semifield S, together with a full classification up to isotopy — a question open since Sandler's foundational work in 1962.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (arXiv:2607.19172v1, by Paolo Santonastaso and Yue Zhou, 2026), where it is presented as a long-standing open problem following Sandler's foundational 1962 work.
solved_when: A complete determination of the autotopism group of every finite cyclic semifield, together with a full resolution of the isotopy problem for this family.
why: A solution would settle a classification question that has stood since Sandler's 1962 foundational work, closing the equivalence problem for one of the central families of finite semifields.

title: On the autotopism groups and the equivalence of finite cyclic semifiel
open: Does there exist a complete classification of cyclic semifields up to isotopism? Only partial results are currently known, and the full solution to the isotopism problem for different cyclic semifields remains open.
solved_when: A full classification of finite cyclic semifields up to isotopism is given, together with a determination of their autotopism groups, resolving the isotopism problem beyond the known partial results.
why: Such a classification would determine when apparently different cyclic semifield constructions are genuinely the same object, and autotopism group data is the basic invariant governing equivalence questions in this area.

title: A complete solution to the Boots-Royle/Cao-Vince conjecture
open: Among all planar graphs on $n \geq 9$ vertices, does $K_2 P_{n-2}$ attain the maximum spectral radius? That is, is the join of an edge with a path on $n-2$ vertices the extremal planar graph for the spectral radius in this range?
solved_when: A proof (or refutation with a counterexample) that $K_2 P_{n-2}$ is the unique planar graph on $n \geq 9$ vertices with maximum spectral radius.
why: It would complete the Boots–Royle/Cao–Vince conjecture, identifying the exact extremal structure governing the spectral radius of planar graphs.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19268v1 (Lele Liu, Bo Ning, Yi Wang)

title: Matchings and Near-Optimal 2-Factor Packings in Percolated Vertex-Tran — conjecture conj:lovasz
open: Does every connected vertex-transitive graph admit a Hamilton path? Equivalently, is there always a spanning path in a connected graph whose automorphism group acts transitively on its vertices?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.20157v2 (Mengyu Cao, Mei Lu, Xiamiao Zhao); no resolution is recorded in the census.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that every connected vertex-transitive graph contains a Hamilton path; the natural criterion for this conjecture is a complete resolution.
why: Hamilton paths in vertex-transitive graphs would settle the long-standing structural intuition that high symmetry forces near-Hamiltonian behavior, constraining how sparse and irregular such graphs can be.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20157v2 (Mengyu Cao, Mei Lu, Xiamiao Zhao)

title: The Erdős-Lovász Tihany Conjecture holds for all even-hole-free graphs — conj c:ELTC
open: Does the Erdős–Lovász Tihany Conjecture hold for every even-hole-free graph? That is, does the conjecture, posed for general graphs, remain true when restricted to graphs containing no even induced cycles?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.20376v1 (Zi-Xia Song).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) of the Erdős–Lovász Tihany Conjecture restricted to the class of even-hole-free graphs is given.
why: Even-hole-free graphs form a structured superclass of chordal graphs, and confirming the conjecture there would extend a classical graph-coloring conjecture to a broad, well-studied hereditary class.

title: The Erdős-Lovász Tihany Conjecture holds for all even-hole-free graphs
open: Does the Erdős–Lovász Tihany Conjecture hold for all even-hole-free graphs? Formally, is it true that every graph with no even hole satisfies the conjecture's chromatic-index divisibility conclusion?
solved_when: The Erdős–Lovász Tihany Conjecture is proved for the class of even-hole-free graphs (or a counterexample within that class is exhibited).
why: It would extend the Tihany conjecture to a major structured graph class, adding to the known verifications for line graphs and related claw-free subclasses.

title: The Erdős-Lovász Tihany Conjecture holds for all even-hole-free graphs
open: Does the Erdős-Lovász Tihany Conjecture hold for every even-hole-free graph? In other words, is it true that even-hole-free graphs also satisfy the conclusions of the conjecture?
status: Stated as an open problem in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.20376v1 (Zi-Xia Song).
solved_when: The conjecture is verified for the class of even-hole-free graphs, i.e., a proof (or counterexample) is given for {c:ELTC} restricted to even-hole-free graphs.
why: Resolving it would extend the Erdős-Lovász Tihany Conjecture to a major structured graph class, and a counterexample would sharply delimit the conjecture's reach.

title: Autonomous disproofs of the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$ wi
open: Can the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$ be disproven by an autonomous (AI-driven) argument rather than by human effort? More precisely, is there a machine-generated counterexample or proof of failure for the conjecture over the real numbers?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.20525v1 (Yichen Huang, http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20525v1).
solved_when: An autonomous system produces a rigorous disproof of the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$ — that is, a verified counterexample or proof of negation accepted as correct.
why: Such a result would mark a milestone in the application of AI to mathematical research, showing that AI systems can resolve long-standing open problems in discrete geometry without human-driven proof discovery.

title: Autonomous disproofs of the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$ wi
open: Can an autonomous research agent independently discover a disproof of the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$, when the truth value is not disclosed to it? Formally, if it is unknown whether the conjecture holds, the agent can be run twice — once instructed to seek a proof, once a disproof — with the hint about the conjecture's truth removed.
solved_when: An autonomous agent, run without the hint about the conjecture's truth (attempting both a proof and a disproof in separate runs, at the cost of approximately doubling the test-time compute), produces a valid disproof of the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$.
why: It would demonstrate that autonomous systems can settle conjectures whose truth value is genuinely unknown, rather than merely reproducing hints seeded by the problem statement.

title: Combinatorial formula for the Moore-Penrose inverse of the complex sig
open: Is there a combinatorial formula for the Moore–Penrose inverse of the complex signature matrix? This resolves the open problem posed in the concluding remarks of Barik et. al.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20658v1 (XiaoYang Liu, Sudipta Mallik, Anh Tang); no solution is recorded.
solved_when: An explicit combinatorial formula for the Moore–Penrose inverse of the complex signature matrix is given and proved.
why: It would extend the combinatorial-linear-algebra toolkit for generalized inverses to the complex signature matrix, closing a question explicitly left open in the literature.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20658v1 (XiaoYang Liu, Sudipta Mallik, Anh Tang)

title: Compactness of abundance in asymmetric hypergraph removal lemmas — question quesGHIM
open: Is a family of graphs triangle-abundant exactly when it contains a triangle-abundant graph? Formally, does a family of $K_3$-coloured graphs being triangle-abundant imply it contains a triangle-abundant $K_3$-coloured graph (and conversely)?
solved_when: Both directions of the equivalence are established: a family of graphs (resp. $K_3$-coloured graphs) is triangle-abundant if and only if it contains a triangle-abundant member.
why: It would pin down how abundance, an asymmetric hypergraph-removal-lemma notion, behaves under compactness — whether the family-level property is witnessed by a single graph.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21640v2 (Shuang Sun, Yan Wang, Yuyao Yang)

title: A class of polyocollection ideals with quadratic Gröbner bases — conj conj1
open: For a collection of cells $P$, is the $h$-polynomial of the polyocollection ideal $K[P]$ equal to the rank-generating polynomial $r_P(t)$, and is its Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity equal to $r(P)$?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) establishing, for every collection of cells $P$, that the $h$-polynomial of $K[P]$ is $r_P(t)$ and that $\operatorname{reg} K[P] = r(P)$.
why: It would tie the homological invariants of these ideals directly to the combinatorial rank data of the cell collection, making regularity and $h$-polynomials computable purely combinatorially.

title: On the Maximality of Additive Codes — prob 5
open: Is the dual system of a nondegenerate additive code an invariant of the code's equivalence class? Formally: if two nondegenerate additive $(n,k,d)_{q^m/q}$-codes are equivalent in the broad, isometric sense of the source paper's Remark, must some collineation carry the dual system of one onto that of the other?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that whenever two nondegenerate additive $(n,k,d)_{q^m/q}$-codes are equivalent in the isometric sense of the paper, a collineation maps one dual system onto the other; a positive answer establishes that additive extendability, like extendability, is invariant under general code equivalence.
why: Additive extendability depends only on the dual system, so invariance of the dual system under equivalence would make additive extendability a well-defined property of equivalence classes, a rigidity result paralleling the known invariance of extendability under code equivalence.

title: Positivity of stretched Littlewood-Richardson coefficients for partiti — conjecture conj:ktt
open: Is every coefficient of the stretched polynomial $P(t)$, expressed in the monomial basis, nonnegative? More precisely, the conjecture asks whether positivity holds coefficient-by-coefficient for the polynomial arising from stretching, not merely that its values at nonnegative integers are nonnegative.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.22301v2 (Alper Ferudun); no progress beyond the statement is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that each monomial-basis coefficient of $P(t)$ is nonnegative; no further quantitative targets are stated in the record.
why: A solution would reveal hidden combinatorial structure in stretched Littlewood–Richardson coefficients, pointing toward a positive, combinatorial model where only polynomiality is currently guaranteed.

title: Tadpole Nahm sum as a Wronskian — conjecture conj:CMP
open: Is the principal tadpole Nahm sum $_r(1,,1;q)$, after multiplication by an appropriate rational power of $q$, a modular function (or form)? In other words, does this $q$-shifted Nahm sum enjoy modularity as conjectured?
status: The problem was stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.22904v1 (Shane Chern, Chanh Tran, Tanay Wakhare); no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) of the modularity of the shifted principal tadpole Nahm sum $_r(1,,1;q)$, establishing the conjecture labeled conj:CMP.
why: Resolving it would place a natural family of tadpole Nahm sums within the theory of modular forms, extending the classical Nahm-sum modularity picture; the conjecture currently stands unproved in the source literature.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22904v1 (Shane Chern, Chanh Tran, Tanay Wakhare)

title: Exact values and exact upper bounds for families of integers with arit — problem prob:kernel
open: Does every extremal family in this problem contain a common element shared by all its members? Computations suggest that for $N \le 12$ the answer is yes, and in fact every maximum family has a common element; the question is whether this holds for every $N$.

solved_when: A proof that for every $N$, some extremal family has a common element — equivalently (by the computations for $N \le 12$), that every maximum extremal family has a common element.
why: Confirming the common-element structure would pin down the exact extremal families and exact values that the source paper's upper bounds aim for, turning bounds into a complete solution.

title: Oddtown and eventown theorems for lattice paths — conjecture conj:catalan
open: Is the number of families of $n$ lattice paths, each of size $2^n$, in which every two distinct paths share an even number of common edges, exactly the Catalan number $C_n$? More precisely, the conjecture asserts a Catalan-type enumeration for this eventown-style condition on lattice paths.
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.23117v1 (Umesh Shanker); no proof is known.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that exactly $C_n$ such families of size $2^n$ exist, where each family consists of lattice paths with every two distinct paths having an even number of common edges.
why: It would extend the classical Oddtown/Eventown theorems to the setting of lattice paths, giving a precise Catalan-number enumeration where only a parity condition is imposed.

title: Nahm Sums Dual to Zagier's Rank-Three Examples and Related Identities
open: Do the conjectural Kanade–Russell identities modulo 9 hold? These identities equate certain double sums with infinite products, and they remain open despite their deceptively simple form.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the conjectural Kanade–Russell identities modulo 9 is given, establishing that the double sums in question equal the stated infinite products.
why: These identities sit at the interface of Nahm sums and q-series, and resolving them would settle a deceptively simple family of conjectures that have resisted proof.

title: A diamond-free claw-free cubic graph with strong chromatic index 7 — problem prob:41
open: Does there exist a diamond-free, claw-free cubic graph whose strong chromatic index is 7?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.23462v1 (Kanishk Raj Tanwar).
solved_when: A diamond-free claw-free cubic graph with strong chromatic index exactly 7 is exhibited, or it is proved that no such graph exists.
why: It would resolve whether the value 7 can occur for the strong chromatic index in this restricted class of cubic graphs, a natural test case for strong-edge-coloring conjectures.

title: Balance Constants, Majority Cycles, and the Gold Partition Conjecture
open: Does Peczarski's broken-rung conjecture hold for all $n \ge 9$? That is, is the conjecture valid for every instance of size at least nine, beyond the range already verified?
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.23926v2 (Anish Gupta); no case beyond those recorded there is reported as settled.
solved_when: The broken-rung conjecture is proved (or refuted) for all $n \ge 9$.
why: A resolution settles a concrete conjecture from the Gold partition and majority-cycle framework, extending known small cases to the general range.

title: Existence of generalized bent functions in the exceptional $q\equiv2\p
open: Do generalized bent functions exist in the exceptional case $q\equiv2$? More precisely, does the open problem on the existence of generalized bent functions stated in the source paper admit a positive answer in this setting?
status: The problem was stated as open in the source paper (2026), available at http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24103v3 (Jianing Li, Shi Ying, Shenxing Zhang).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the existence of generalized bent functions in the exceptional $q\equiv2$ case, resolving the open problem as stated in the source paper.

key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24103v3 (Jianing Li, Shi Ying, Shenxing Zhang)

title: Existence of generalized bent functions in the exceptional $q\equiv2\p
open: Do generalized bent functions of type $(m,q)$ exist in the exceptional case where $m$ is odd and $q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$? Kumar, Scholtz, and Welch constructed such functions whenever $m$ is even or $q \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, leaving exactly this remaining case open.
status: The problem was stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.24103v3 (Jianing Li, Shi Ying, Shenxing Zhang). Kumar, Scholtz, and Welch constructed generalized bent functions for $m$ even or $q \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$; the case $m$ odd and $q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ remains unresolved.
solved_when: An explicit construction (or a proof of existence, or of nonexistence) of a generalized bent function of type $(m,q)$ for every odd $m$ and every $q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$.
why: It would complete the classification of which types $(m,q)$ admit generalized bent functions, settling the last case left open since the original construction of Kumar, Scholtz, and Welch.

title: When Do Subset Sums in Finite Abelian Groups Support $2$-Designs?
open: Which finite abelian groups have subset sums that can carry a nontrivial $2$-design? More precisely, can such a nontrivial $2$-design exist unless the underlying group is an elementary abelian $p$-group?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) settling, for every finite abelian group, whether a nontrivial $2$-design on its subset sums can exist only when the group is elementary abelian.
why: It would characterize exactly which finite abelian groups support $2$-designs built from subset sums, sharpening the structural constraints on combinatorial designs over these groups.

title: The $K(π, 1)$ conjecture for Artin groups of spherical type
open: For every Coxeter group $W$, is the associated space $Y_W$ a $K(G_W, 1)$ — that is, does its universal cover become contractible for the Artin group $G_W$ attached to $W$?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that $Y_W$ is a $K(G_W, 1)$ for every Coxeter group $W$.
why: This is a central structural statement about Artin groups; establishing it for all Coxeter groups would settle the $K(\pi, 1)$ property uniformly, unlocking homological and geometric tools that currently must be verified type by type.

title: Exponentially Many Circuit Double Covers — conjecture conj:CDC
open: Does every bridgeless cubic graph admit a circuit double cover — specifically, a cycle double cover (equivalently, a circuit double cover)? More broadly, the conjecture asks whether such covers exist not just singly but in exponentially many forms.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), available at http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24724v1 (Radek Hušek, Robert Šámal).
solved_when: A proof that every bridgeless cubic graph has a cycle double cover (equivalently, a circuit double cover); for the "exponentially many" strengthening, a proof that the number of distinct covers grows exponentially with the graph.
why: Resolving it would settle a foundational existence question about how cycles can uniformly cover bridgeless cubic graphs, a core case of the general circuit double cover problem.

title: Exponentially Many Circuit Double Covers — conjecture conj:manyCiDCs
open: Does every 2-connected cubic graph on $n$ vertices admit exponentially many circuit double covers? Conjecturally, at least $2^{n/2 - 1}$ circuit double covers exist for every such graph.
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper arXiv:2607.24724v1 (Radek Hušek, Robert Šámal), published 2026; no resolution is recorded in the census.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every 2-connected cubic graph on $n$ vertices has at least $2^{n/2 - 1}$ circuit double covers.
why: It would strengthen the classical circuit double cover conjecture from mere existence to abundance, showing such covers are not rare exceptions but come in exponential families.

title: Exponentially Many Circuit Double Covers — conjecture conj:5CDC
open: Does every bridgeless cubic graph admit a double cover by five circuits? That is, does the 5-Circuit Double Cover (5-CyDC) conjecture hold for all bridgeless cubic graphs?
solved_when: A proof that every bridgeless cubic graph has a 5-CyDC (or a counterexample exhibiting a bridgeless cubic graph with no such cover).
why: It is a natural strengthening of the classical circuit double cover conjecture, pinning down the number of covering circuits to five; a proof would settle the structure of cycle covers in cubic graphs more precisely.

title: The Mendez-Pinto-Villarreal Conjecture for some classes of monomial id
open: Which cubic square-free monomial ideals have the Simis property? A complete characterization of the Simis property for this class of ideals is still missing.
status: Stated as an open problem in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.25683v1 (Paromita Bordoloi, Kanoy Kumar Das, Rajiv Kumar).
solved_when: A complete combinatorial characterization of cubic square-free monomial ideals satisfying the Simis property is given, with proof.
why: It would settle a natural boundary case of the Mendez-Pinto-Villarreal Conjecture, telling commutative algebraists exactly which hypergraphs attached to cubic square-free ideals are normal.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25683v1 (Paromita Bordoloi, Kanoy Kumar Das, Rajiv Kumar)

title: Constructing two completely independent spanning trees in dual-cubes
open: If the $n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_n$ admits $k$ completely independent spanning trees, must the dual-cube $F_{n+1}$ also admit $k$ completely independent spanning trees? In other words, does the hypercube construction lift to the dual-cube of the next dimension?
status: Stated as an open problem in the source paper (2026), Mohammed Lalou, Nader Mbarek, Abdallah Skender, arXiv:2607.25917v2. No progress beyond the statement is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit counterexample) of the implication: whenever $Q_n$ has $k$ completely independent spanning trees, $F_{n+1}$ has $k$ completely independent spanning trees.
why: It would give a general mechanism for porting completely independent spanning trees from hypercubes into dual-cubes, advancing the construction of such trees in this network family.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25917v2 (Mohammed Lalou, Nader Mbarek, Abdallah Skender)

title: Rank Contributions of Vertices in Rigidity Matroids of Clique Covered — conjecture con:zeo
open: Is every 6-connected graph whose edges are covered by copies of $K_4$ rigid in $\mathbb{R}^3$?
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the statement that every $6$-connected $K_4$-covered graph is rigid in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
why: It would extend the characterization of rigidity from combinatorial structure to connectivity-based sufficient conditions in three dimensions, where no combinatorial characterization of rigidity is known.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26266v1 (Bill Jackson, Tibor Jordán, Soma Villányi)

title: Rank Contributions of Vertices in Rigidity Matroids of Clique Covered — conjecture con:zeo2
open: Is every $6$-connected, 3-dimensional combinatorial zeolite globally rigid in $\mathbb{R}^3$? In other words, does this level of connectivity suffice to force global rigidity for this class of frameworks?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that every $6$-connected, 3-dimensional combinatorial zeolite is globally rigid in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is given.
why: Resolving it would extend global rigidity theory to the zeolite class of body–bar-type structures, a natural family of 3-dimensional frameworks where the usual sufficient conditions are not known to apply.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26266v1 (Bill Jackson, Tibor Jordán, Soma Villányi)

title: Finitely additive measures on $\mathbb Z$ and additive combinatorics
open: Is there an almost translation-invariant, finitely additive measure on $\mathbb Z$ that is neither an ultrafilter measure nor fully translation-invariant? In other words, does the class of almost translation-invariant measures strictly contain the two known kinds?
status: The question is stated as open in the source paper, arXiv:2607.26522v1 (Zeinab Ashtab, David Fernández-Bretón), 2026; no partial results are recorded.
solved_when: An explicit (or existence) construction of an almost translation-invariant finitely additive measure on $\mathbb Z$ is given that is neither an ultrafilter measure nor translation-invariant; a proof that no such measure exists would equally settle the question.
why: It would clarify the structure of almost translation-invariant measures on $\mathbb Z$ and delimit the reach of ultrafilter-based constructions in additive combinatorics.

title: Fuglede's Conjecture on Cyclic Groups of Square-Free Order: The Case o
open: Does Fuglede's conjecture hold for finite cyclic groups — in particular, is there an infinite family of cyclic groups, with an arbitrarily large number of distinct divisors, for which spectral sets and tiles coincide? Following recent preprints, the conjecture remains open only for finite cyclic groups, and until now no such infinite family was known. Let MATH be a bounded measurable set of positive measure.
solved_when: An infinite family of finite cyclic groups, possessing an arbitrary number of distinct divisors, is established for which Fuglede's conjecture holds (i.e., every spectral set in the group tiles it and vice versa).
why: It would reduce the last remaining setting of Fuglede's conjecture to explicit arithmetic structure on cyclic groups, connecting spectral sets and tilings where the problem is now known to survive.

title: Hadwiger's conjecture for hypergraphs
open: Is Hadwiger's conjecture true — that is, must every finite graph $G$ satisfy the conclusion of the conjecture?
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of Hadwiger's conjecture as stated for finite graphs.
why: Resolving Hadwiger's conjecture would settle one of the deepest open problems in graph coloring and graph minors, unifying chromatic number and clique-minor structure.

title: Schur Eisenstein series and Schur MacMahon series
open: Do the Schur MacMahon series span the entire space of quasimodular forms with integral coefficients? In other words, is every integral-coefficient quasimodular form expressible as an integral linear combination of these series, which arise from two families of quasimodular forms indexed by partitions?
status: The conjecture that the Schur MacMahon series span all quasimodular forms with integral coefficients is stated as open in the source paper (2026), Henrik Bachmann and Jinbo Yu, arXiv:2607.27702v1.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) that the Schur MacMahon series span all quasimodular forms with integral coefficients.
why: It would establish these partition-indexed series as a generating framework for integral quasimodular forms, with the Schur Eisenstein series providing the symmetric-function bridge connecting the two families.

title: The Multiset Dimension of Graphs: Extremal Values and King Grids — problem prob:struct
open: Which graphs attain the largest possible multiset dimension, md(G) = n(G)? All eight currently known examples have diameter 3 and girth 3, so a natural goal is to characterize such graphs or at least exhibit an infinite family — and to determine whether diameter 3 is necessary, up to finitely many exceptions.
solved_when: A characterization of graphs with md(G) = n(G) is given, or an infinite family of such graphs is constructed; additionally, an answer to whether diameter 3 is required apart from finitely many exceptions.
why: It would settle the extremal behavior of the multiset dimension, clarifying how large this parameter can be relative to graph order and which structural properties force equality.

title: The Aldous property for normal Cayley graphs on symmetric groups — prob prob
open: Which Cayley graphs on the symmetric group $S_n$ possess the Aldous property? A complete characterization — determining exactly which of these graphs satisfy the property — is the goal.
solved_when: An explicit description of all Cayley graphs on $S_n$ having the Aldous property is given, with proof that the listed graphs all have the property and that no others do.
why: It would settle a natural classification question about the interchange process on symmetric groups, telling us exactly when the worst-case relaxation behavior is governed by transpositions.

title: Structure of 2-step nilpotent ergodic averages for distinct-degree pol — conjecture Conj: popular common differences
open: Do the conclusions of the source paper's theorem and corollary extend from the special monomial family to a nilpotent system of arbitrary step, with all independent polynomials in place of the distinct-degree monomials currently treated?
solved_when: The theorem and corollary of the source paper are established for nilpotent systems/groups of arbitrary step and all independent polynomials, not only the distinct-degree monomial case.
why: It would complete the structural picture of nilpotent ergodic averages for polynomial sequences, removing the restriction to monomials of distinct degrees.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29368v2 (Andreas Koutsogiannis, Borys Kuca, Wenbo Sun)

title: Structure of 2-step nilpotent ergodic averages for distinct-degree pol — problem Pr: distinct-degree pointwise
open: For a nilpotent system $(X,\mu,T_1,\dots,T_\ell)$ and nonconstant polynomials $p_1,\dots,p_\ell$ of pairwise distinct degrees, do the corresponding multiple ergodic averages converge pointwise almost everywhere for arbitrary $L^\infty(\mu)$ functions? A precise positive answer would establish the structure and convergence of 2-step nilpotent ergodic averages over distinct-degree polynomials.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper "http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29368v2" (Andreas Koutsogiannis, Borys Kuca, Wenbo Sun), from paper 2607.29368, presented as a curated open problem (2026). No progress beyond the statement is recorded.
solved_when: For every nilpotent system, every tuple of nonconstant distinct-degree polynomials, and all functions $f_1,\dots,f_\ell \in L^\infty(\mu)$, the averages converge for $\mu$-a.e. $x \in X$.
why: Pointwise convergence of these averages extends classical ergodic-theoretic results to the nilpotent, distinct-degree polynomial setting, a basic case where general pointwise convergence results are currently missing.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29368v2 (Andreas Koutsogiannis, Borys Kuca, Wenbo Sun)

title: Structure of 2-step nilpotent ergodic averages for distinct-degree pol — problem Pr: nilpotent joint ergodicity criteria on nilsystems
open: When are finitely many polynomials jointly ergodic on a nilsystem, and can this be detected by reducing to the abelianization? Formally: given totally ergodic nilrotations $S_1, \dots, S_$ on a $k$-step nilsystem $(Y, _Y, m_Y)$ generating an $s$-step nilpotent group, with $Y=G/$, lower central series filtration $(G_i)_{i _0}$, and $Y_i := G/(G_{i+1})$ for every $n _0$, show that the polynomials $p_1, \dots, p_$ are jointly ergodic on $Y$ if and only if they are jointly ergodic on $Y_s$.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given of the equivalence: joint ergodicity of $p_1, \dots, p_$ on $Y$ holds exactly when it holds on the quotient $Y_s$.
why: It would reduce joint ergodicity questions on nilsystems to the corresponding question on their top quotient, giving a workable nilpotent analogue of joint ergodicity criteria; without it, no general criterion is available beyond lower-step cases.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29368v2 (Andreas Koutsogiannis, Borys Kuca, Wenbo Sun)

title: Strong invariants and Tverberg numbers in convexity spaces
open: Can the Tverberg number with tolerance $t$ in dimension $2$, namely $r_t^{(2)}$, be bounded in terms of the tolerance-free value $r_2^{(2)}$ alone? More precisely, does there exist a function of $r_2^{(2)}$ that upper-bounds $r_t^{(2)}$ uniformly?
status: The question is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.29403v1 (Minho Cho, Andreas F. Holmsen, Attila Jung).
solved_when: An explicit bound $r_t^{(2)} \le f(r_2^{(2)})$ is established for some function $f$, or a counterexample showing no such function exists is constructed.
why: Such a bound would show tolerance Tverberg numbers in the plane are controlled by the classical parameter, yielding quantitative results for convexity-space analogues of Tverberg's theorem.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29403v1 (Minho Cho, Andreas F. Holmsen, Attila Jung)

title: On some perfect matching conjectures in infinite, cubic, bridgeless gr — conj conjecture4
open: Does every bridgeless cubic graph admit two perfect matchings $M_1, M_2$ such that the graph $G(M_1 M_2)$ is bipartite?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that in every bridgeless cubic graph such a pair of perfect matchings $M_1, M_2$ exists with $G(M_1 M_2)$ bipartite.
why: The conjecture sits in the circle of perfect matching conjectures for infinite, cubic, bridgeless graphs, where matching guarantees are central to structural and decomposition questions; resolving it clarifies how perfect matchings can be paired to control the structure of the graph they generate.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29511v1 (Paulo Magalhães Júnior, Antonio Kelson Silva)

title: On some perfect matching conjectures in infinite, cubic, bridgeless gr — conj conjecture1
open: Does every infinite, bridgeless, cubic graph admit six perfect matchings such that each edge is contained in exactly two of them? Equivalently, is the corresponding perfect-matching-cover conjecture true in the infinite setting?
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.29511v1 (Paulo Magalhães Júnior, Antonio Kelson Silva).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the statement that every bridgeless cubic graph — finite or infinite — has six perfect matchings covering each edge exactly twice.
why: It extends the classical perfect matching covering conjectures for cubic graphs to the infinite case, where compactness arguments fail and new techniques are needed.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29511v1 (Paulo Magalhães Júnior, Antonio Kelson Silva)

title: On some perfect matching conjectures in infinite, cubic, bridgeless gr — conj conjecture2
open: Does every bridgeless cubic graph admit three perfect matchings whose intersection is empty — that is, perfect matchings $M_1, M_2, M_3$ such that no edge belongs to all three?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that every bridgeless cubic graph $G$ contains three perfect matchings $M_1, M_2, M_3$ with no edge covered by all of them.
why: It would refine our understanding of how perfect matchings overlap in bridgeless cubic graphs, a setting central to classical matching conjectures such as the Berge–Fulkerson-type questions; a counterexample would expose a structural obstruction.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29511v1 (Paulo Magalhães Júnior, Antonio Kelson Silva)

title: On some perfect matching conjectures in infinite, cubic, bridgeless gr — conj conjecture3
open: Does every bridgeless cubic graph admit two perfect matchings $M_1, M_2$ whose product $M_1 M_2$ contains no odd edge-cut? In other words, can a pair of perfect matchings always be chosen so that the symmetric structure they generate avoids odd edge-cuts entirely?
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2607.29511v1, by Paulo Magalhães Júnior and Antonio Kelson Silva; no progress beyond the statement is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that every bridgeless cubic graph contains two perfect matchings $M_1, M_2$ such that $M_1 M_2$ does not contain an odd edge-cut.
why: A positive answer would strengthen the classical perfect matching theory for cubic bridgeless graphs, constraining how pairs of perfect matchings can interact with edge-cuts; a counterexample would reveal new structural limits on such pairs.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29511v1 (Paulo Magalhães Júnior, Antonio Kelson Silva)

title: On the Integer Domination Root Conjecture
open: Must every integer root of the domination polynomial $D(G,x)$ of a graph $G$ belong to the set $\{0,-2\}$? In other words, if $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ is an integer root of $D(G,x)$, must $x \in \{0,-2\}$?
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper, "On the Integer Domination Root Conjecture" (Saeid Alikhani, Max Griswold), available at http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00109v1.
solved_when: A proof, or a counterexample, is given: either every integer root of $D(G,x)$ is shown to lie in $\{0,-2\}$ for all graphs $G$, or some graph is exhibited whose domination polynomial has an integer root outside $\{0,-2\}$.
why: Resolving it would settle a basic question about the arithmetic of domination polynomials and constrain the possible integer zeros these counting polynomials can attain.

title: Antimagic orientations of graphs with a dominating clique — conjecture conj:hr
open: Does every connected graph other than $K_2$ admit an antimagic orientation — that is, can its edges be oriented and labeled bijectively so that vertex sums are all distinct? In formal terms, is every connected graph $G \neq K_2$ antimagic?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), available at http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00209v1 (Abdulrahman Al-Taweel).
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that every connected graph other than $K_2$ admits an antimagic labeling via orientation.
why: Settling it would resolve a natural, broadly studied extremal case of the antimagic labeling program and clarify exactly which small graphs obstruct antimagicness.

title: Antimagic orientations of graphs with a dominating clique — conjecture conj:hms
open: Does every connected graph admit an antimagic orientation? That is, can the edges of any connected graph be oriented and labeled with distinct labels so that the resulting vertex sums are all distinct?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2608.00209v1 (Abdulrahman Al-Taweel); the record lists no further results.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the statement that every connected graph admits an antimagic orientation; partial progress should specify exactly which graph classes are settled, such as graphs with a dominating clique.
why: It would settle a general conjecture on antimagic labelings and, in particular, resolve the dominating-clique case raised in the source paper.

title: The finitude of the fibers of the complementary Bell numbers — problem 5.7 2
open: Are the fibers of the complementary Bell numbers finite? That is, does each value occur only finitely many times among the complementary Bell numbers?
status: The problem, attributed to Subbarao and Verma, is stated as open in the source paper (2026), "From paper 2608.00575" (John M. Campbell, http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00575v1); no partial results are recorded in the census.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every fiber of the complementary Bell number sequence is finite is given; equivalently, for each value, the set of indices at which the complementary Bell numbers take that value is shown to be finite (or a counterexample exhibited).
why: This is Problem 5.7(2), attributed to Subbarao and Verma, and resolving it settles a basic structural question about the value distribution of the complementary Bell numbers.

title: Binary X-rays of doubly stochastic matrices — question question
open: Which vectors in $\mathbb{Z}^n$ can be expressed as the sum of two permutations $\pi$ and $\sigma$ of $[n] = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, where each permutation is written as a vector in one-line notation? Equivalently, one asks for a characterization of the integer vectors that arise as the "binary X-ray" — coordinatewise sum — of two permutation vectors.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2608.01442v2 (Bangzheng Li, Yuewei Liu, Yuan Yao); no partial resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A complete characterization of the set of vectors in $\mathbb{Z}^n$ that can be written as the sum of two permutations of $[n]$ (in one-line notation) is given, together with a proof of its correctness.
why: This characterizes the possible degree sequences of bipartite graphs decomposable into two perfect matchings, a basic structural question at the interface of combinatorics and doubly stochastic matrices.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01442v2 (Bangzheng Li, Yuewei Liu, Yuan Yao)

title: Binary X-rays of doubly stochastic matrices — conjecture conj:binary
open: If a score vector contains no duplicate values, must its frequency vector always be realizable as the X-ray of a permutation?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given: for every score vector with all distinct entries, the associated frequency vector arises as the X-ray of a permutation; equivalently, a single duplicated-value example refuting it.
why: It would characterize exactly which frequency data of doubly stochastic matrices comes from permutations, sharpening the structural theory of binary X-rays.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01442v2 (Bangzheng Li, Yuewei Liu, Yuan Yao)

title: Binary X-rays of doubly stochastic matrices — conjecture conj:ds-to-perm
open: If a binary vector in $\mathbb{R}^{2n-1}$ arises as the X-ray of a doubly stochastic matrix, must it also arise as the X-ray of a permutation matrix? In other words, does every doubly stochastic X-ray already come from a permutation matrix?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for all $n$ and all binary vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{2n-1}$.
why: It would characterize exactly which binary X-rays are achievable by doubly stochastic matrices, reducing the doubly stochastic case to the discrete, combinatorial setting of permutation matrices.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01442v2 (Bangzheng Li, Yuewei Liu, Yuan Yao)

title: The DP Color Function of Bipartite Graphs
open: For every graph, does its DP color function eventually agree with some polynomial — that is, is there a threshold beyond which the function is given exactly by a polynomial at all larger values? Formally, as stated in the source: for every graph $G$, is there an $n_0$ and a polynomial $P$ such that $P_{DP}(G,k) = P(k)$ whenever $k \geq n_0$?
status: The question is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2608.02335v1 (Hemanshu Kaul, Jeffrey A. Mudrock, Gunjan Sharma).
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that for every graph $G$ there exist an $n_0$ and a polynomial $P$ with $P_{DP}(G,k) = P(k)$ for all $k \geq n_0$; the record states no further quantitative targets.
why: The chromatic polynomial of a graph is always a polynomial, while the DP color function can deviate from it; establishing eventual polynomiality would clarify precisely how DP-coloring counts behave for large numbers of colors.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02335v1 (Hemanshu Kaul, Jeffrey A. Mudrock, Gunjan Sharma)

title: On Hamilton cycles in connected vertex-transitive graphs of order $2pq
open: If a vertex-transitive graph is Hamiltonian, must every edge of it lie on some Hamilton cycle?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2608.02349v2 (Zhou Tianlei); no partial results are recorded.
solved_when: A proof that, in every Hamiltonian vertex-transitive graph, each edge is contained in at least one Hamilton cycle — or a counterexample exhibiting a Hamiltonian vertex-transitive graph with an edge in no Hamilton cycle.
why: It would reveal how tightly Hamiltonicity in vertex-transitive graphs constrains the structure of the full set of Hamilton cycles, beyond mere existence.

title: Locally bipartite subgraphs via multicolor Ramsey numbers
open: Can high-chromatic graphs of large girth be found everywhere, rather than merely shown to exist? An old conjecture of Erdős and Hajnal, going back to at least 1969, asserts that every graph of sufficiently large chromatic number contains a subgraph that is both high-chromatic and of large girth — making such graphs ubiquitous, not just existent as Erdős originally proved.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), a curated open-problems paper by Raphael Steiner (http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02522v2), where it is described as amongst the most famous open problems in this direction; the conjecture, due to Erdős and Hajnal, goes back to at least 1969.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture: for every target chromatic number and girth, there exists a threshold chromatic number such that every graph whose chromatic number exceeds the threshold contains a subgraph with the target chromatic number and girth.
why: It would upgrade the classic probabilistic existence of high-chromatic, large-girth graphs into a structural guarantee inside every highly chromatic graph, a fundamental step in understanding how chromatic number and local sparsity interact.

title: On (1,1,2,3)- and (1,1,3,3,3)-Packing Colorings of Claw-Free Subcubic
open: Is every connected claw-free subcubic graph other than a single exception $H$ admits a $(1,1,3,3,4)$-packing coloring? Formally: does every connected claw-free subcubic graph $G \not\cong H$ admit a $(1,1,3,3,4)$-packing coloring?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2608.02566v1 by Maidoun Mortada, Ayman El Zein, and Sara Al Hajjar.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that every connected claw-free subcubic graph distinct from $H$ is $(1,1,3,3,4)$-packing colorable; a counterexample suffices to resolve it negatively.
why: It would settle the packing-colorability boundary for claw-free subcubic graphs under this specific color-distance pattern, complementing the $(1,1,2,3)$- and $(1,1,3,3,3)$-colorings studied in the same paper.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02566v1 (Maidoun Mortada, Ayman El Zein, Sara Al Hajjar)

title: On (1,1,2,3)- and (1,1,3,3,3)-Packing Colorings of Claw-Free Subcubic
open: Is every subcubic graph other than the Petersen graph $(1,1,2,3)$-packing colorable? Equivalently, can the vertices of any such graph be colored with two colors of distance 1 and one color each of distances 2 and 3?
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit counterexample other than the Petersen graph) of the statement that all subcubic graphs except the Petersen graph admit a $(1,1,2,3)$-packing coloring.
why: It would pin down the exact packing-colorability threshold for subcubic graphs under this color pattern, completing one of the natural cases left open in the packing coloring of sparse graphs.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02566v1 (Maidoun Mortada, Ayman El Zein, Sara Al Hajjar)

title: On (1,1,2,3)- and (1,1,3,3,3)-Packing Colorings of Claw-Free Subcubic
open: Every claw-free subcubic graph is $(1,2,2,2,2)$-packing colorable.
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2608.02566v1 by Maidoun Mortada, Ayman El Zein, and Sara Al Hajjar; no progress beyond its statement is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that every claw-free subcubic graph admits a $(1,2,2,2,2)$-packing coloring.
why: It would settle the third conjecture of the source paper on packing colorings of claw-free subcubic graphs, extending the reach of packing coloring to a natural graph class defined by forbidden induced claws and maximum degree 3.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02566v1 (Maidoun Mortada, Ayman El Zein, Sara Al Hajjar)

title: Two-Sided Dimension Bounds for the Peterson Hit Problem via Projection
open: For the Peterson hit problem in five or more variables, can the dimensions of the hit (or indecomposable) spaces be determined in every degree, rather than only in specified degrees and for generic families?
solved_when: A determination of the Peterson hit problem dimensions is achieved in all degrees for five or more variables, extending the currently known complete answers in specified degrees and generic families.
why: A full-degree determination would complete the dimension theory of the hit problem in the remaining range of variables, where only partial cases are currently settled.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02623v3 (Dang Vo Phuc, Peter V. Danchev)

title: Zero-error expectation equals amortized query complexity
open: Does the zero-error expected query complexity of a function equal its amortized query complexity? A formal answer would characterize precisely when allowing shared randomness and batching across many instances does not help beyond solving each instance in expectation.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation, with counterexample) of the equality between zero-error expected query complexity and amortized query complexity, as posed in open problem 2 of the source paper.
why: An answer would settle whether amortization fundamentally reduces the query cost of zero-error computation, informing lower-bound and algorithm-design techniques in query complexity.

title: All parallel chip-firing games with $2|E|-|V|<|σ|<2|E|$ have period $2 — conj conj:jlw
open: Does every parallel chip-firing game whose total chip count $\sigma$ satisfies $2|E|-|V|<|\sigma|<2|E|$ have period 2? In other words, in this intermediate chip-density regime, is the eventual dynamics always a 2-cycle?
solved_when: A proof (or a counterexample) is given that all parallel chip-firing games with $2|E|-|V|<|\sigma|<2|E|$ are eventually periodic with period 2.
why: It would complete the classification of parallel chip-firing behavior by chip density, pinning down the exact boundary of the period-2 regime.

title: On the Burgess bound and Pythagorean triples involving primitive roots — conjecture Conj. primitive
open: Is it true that for every prime $p>7$ there is a right triangle whose side lengths all lie in $\{1,2,\dots,p-1\}$ and whose area is exactly a primitive root modulo $p$?
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) of the existence, for every prime $p>7$, of a right triangle with all side lengths in $\{1,2,\dots,p-1\}$ whose area is a primitive root modulo $p$.
why: It connects the classical theory of Pythagorean triples with the multiplicative structure of finite fields, testing how far the distribution of primitive roots constrains areas of integer right triangles.

title: Cardinal Grid Slime Trail is PSPACE-Complete
open: Is Slime Trail, played with eight-directional movement on a square grid exactly as in competition, computationally intractable? Formally, is this version of the game PSPACE-complete, as posed in the source paper?
status: The problem was stated as open in the source paper (2026), http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05118v1 (Anne Pham, Matthew Ferland).
solved_when: A proof establishes PSPACE-completeness (membership in PSPACE plus hardness) for Slime Trail with eight-directional movement on a square grid, as featured in the Portuguese National Mathematical Games Championship (CNJM) organized by Ludus.
why: It settles the complexity of the game in the form people actually play it, rather than an idealized variant, closing the gap between theory and competition practice.

title: On the Asymptotic Normality and Unimodality of Genus Distributions of — conjecture c1:2
