solved_when: An exact value (or matching upper and lower bounds) is established for the smallest avoidable length of a monochromatic diffsequence under a 3-coloring.
why: This pinpoints the quantitative boundary of Ramsey-type behavior for diffsequences under 3 colors, closing the natural parameter left open in the source problem.

title: Autonomous phase discovery
open: Can we enumerate the accessible Chern sectors of the generalized QWZ model, and can a prescribed Chern number be realized by an explicit construction? Unlike the generalized cluster chain, where both the number of phases and explicit representatives of each phase are known in advance, no such enumeration or general construction is known for the generalized QWZ model.
solved_when: A complete enumeration of the accessible Chern sectors of the generalized QWZ model is given, together with a general construction realizing any prescribed Chern number from that enumeration.
why: It would close the gap between the generalized QWZ model and the generalized cluster chain, where the phase structure is fully characterized, and enable targeted preparation of topological phases with chosen Chern numbers.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33802v1 (Shiyu Zhou, Yuxuan Zhang, Sebastian Wetzel)

title: On the Relation Between Interval Regret and Dynamic Regret
open: Does the relationship between interval regret and dynamic regret run deep enough that a reduction can deliver an efficient, proper algorithm achieving optimal dynamic regret for exp-concave losses over arbitrary compact convex domains? Resolving this would answer a question explicitly left open in the source paper.
solved_when: An explicit, computationally efficient, proper algorithm is shown to attain the optimal dynamic regret for exp-concave losses on arbitrary compact convex domains, via (or independently of) the interval-regret-to-dynamic-regret connection.
why: It would close a stated gap in online convex optimization, giving the first efficient and proper procedure with optimal dynamic regret guarantees for exp-concave losses beyond restricted domains.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34423v1 (Yi-Han Wang, Peng Zhao, Zhi-Hua Zhou)

title: Higher dimensional local class field theory
open: In the setting of the source paper with $d=2$, is there a geometric proof of the stated fact?
status: The question is stated as open in the source paper (2026), Morten Lübers, http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34437v1.
solved_when: A geometric proof is given, in the notation of the source paper with $d=2$, of the fact identified there.
why: It would supply a geometric route to a result currently obtained non-geometrically within higher dimensional local class field theory.

title: Higher dimensional local class field theory — conjecture conjecture2
open: Is the residue map $res$ an isomorphism for arbitrary dimension $d$ in higher dimensional local class field theory? Formally, the conjecture asserts that $res$ is an isomorphism for all $d$, extending beyond the cases already established.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.34437v1 (Morten Lüders).
solved_when: The map $res$ is proven to be an isomorphism for arbitrary $d$.
why: A proof would complete higher dimensional local class field theory by establishing the conjectured reciprocity isomorphism in full generality, removing the restriction to special dimensions.

title: Polylogarithmic Nash Regret in Matrix Games with Bandit Feedback
open: Can a learner achieve instance-dependent polylogarithmic Nash regret in arbitrary finite matrix games with bandit payoff feedback and observed opponent actions?
status: The question was stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.34812v1 (Yuheng Zhang); the record indicates it has since been answered affirmatively, resolving the open problem.
solved_when: An algorithm is exhibited that attains instance-dependent polylogarithmic Nash regret in arbitrary finite matrix games under bandit payoff feedback with observed opponent actions.
why: It establishes whether the fine-grained, instance-dependent guarantees known in related settings extend to the full generality of finite matrix games with bandit feedback, closing a stated gap in that line of work.

title: Polylogarithmic Nash Regret in Matrix Games with Bandit Feedback
open: Can a learning algorithm for matrix games with bandit feedback achieve polylogarithmic Nash regret in arbitrary dimensions? That is, does there exist a method whose Nash regret grows only polylogarithmically in the number of rounds, uniformly over arbitrary game dimensions, when players observe only bandit feedback?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.34812v1 (Yuheng Zhang); no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: An algorithm is given that attains polylogarithmic Nash regret (regret polylogarithmic in the time horizon) under bandit feedback for matrix games of arbitrary dimension, with a proof of its guarantee.
why: It would settle the rate at which Nash convergence is possible with the minimal, bandit-only information structure, closing the gap between what is achievable with richer feedback and what bandit feedback permits.

title: Polylogarithmic Nash Regret in Matrix Games with Bandit Feedback
open: Is instance-dependent polylogarithmic Nash regret achievable in arbitrary matrix games under bandit payoff feedback when the opponent's actions are observed? Formally, the question asks for an algorithm whose instance-dependent Nash regret grows only polylogarithmically in the horizon in this setting.
solved_when: An algorithm is given that attains instance-dependent polylogarithmic Nash regret in arbitrary matrix games with bandit payoff feedback and observed opponent actions, together with a proof.
why: The source paper's Theorem resolves this question, so confirming or refuting it settles whether the polylogarithmic regret barrier can be reached in the bandit-feedback matrix-game setting.

title: A proof of the generalized packing-covering conjecture — conjecture conj:packing-covering
open: Does the generalized packing-covering conjecture hold for finite-field linear codes — that is, is there a sharp relationship between the generalized packing and covering radii of an $[n,k]_q$ linear code? A resolution would establish the conjecture in the form stated for linear codes over finite fields.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) of the generalized packing-covering conjecture, as stated in the source paper, for $[n,k]_q$ linear codes.
why: It would settle a basic structural question about how packing and covering parameters of linear codes constrain each other, informing bounds on codes for error correction.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34910v1 (Gianira N. Alfarano, Giuseppe Marino, Alessandro Neri)

title: Antimagicness of join graphs — conj 1
open: Is every connected graph other than $K_2$ antimagic, meaning its edges can be labeled with distinct integers so that vertex sums are pairwise distinct? This is the join-graph instance of the classical antimagic labeling conjecture.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that every connected graph except $K_2$ admits an antimagic labeling is given.
why: It would settle a foundational conjecture on distinguishing vertices by edge-label sums and extend the known antimagicness results toward the full class of connected graphs.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35245v1 (Grégoire Beaudoire, Cédric Bentz, Christophe Picouleau)

title: Antimagicness of join graphs
open: Which disconnected cographs admit antimagic labelings? A satisfying answer would give a full characterization of antimagic disconnected cographs, including the case where the graph is a disjoint union of complete bipartite graphs.
solved_when: A characterization of the disconnected cographs that are antimagic is proved, covering also the case of a disjoint union of complete bipartite graphs.
why: Completing the characterization closes the remaining gap in the classification of antimagic cographs, turning partial results into a definitive structural theorem for this graph class.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35245v1 (Grégoire Beaudoire, Cédric Bentz, Christophe Picouleau)

title: Disproof of the dominating Hadwiger conjecture
open: Does the dominating Hadwiger conjecture — raised as an open problem by Illingworth and Wood — actually hold? The source paper answers this in the negative, adding the conjecture to the list of failed strengthenings of Hadwiger's conjecture.
status: The problem was stated as open in the source paper (2026); the paper presents a disproof of the conjecture. Key work: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35361v1 (Freddie Illingworth, Raphael Steiner).
solved_when: A rigorous construction (or proof of impossibility) establishing that the dominating Hadwiger conjecture fails, i.e., a disproof appearing in the record is confirmed valid.
why: It extends the list of known failed strengthenings of Hadwiger's conjecture, clarifying which strengthenings remain plausible targets for graph-minor theory.

title: Disproof of the dominating Hadwiger conjecture
open: Does every graph with minimum degree at least k contain a dominating K_k-model? This "dominating Hadwiger conjecture," asked as an open problem by Illingworth and Wood, is significantly stronger than Hadwiger's original conjecture.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the statement: for every positive integer k, every graph of minimum degree at least k contains a dominating K_k-model. The record states no further quantitative targets.
why: A proof would strengthen Hadwiger's conjecture to a dominating version; the case k = 4 was proved by Girão et al., providing a significant strengthening of the four colour theorem.

title: A simple proof of the group-theoretic Zhang-Yeung inequality
open: Is there a simple, direct proof of the group-theoretic Zhang–Yeung inequality, which relates the cardinalities of subgroups of a finite group in the same way the Zhang–Yeung entropy inequality generalizes Shannon's submodularity inequality? Formally, can the inequality for subgroup cardinalities be established using only elementary group-theoretic and counting arguments?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), "A simple proof of the group-theoretic Zhang-Yeung inequality" by Harold Nieuwboer and Lubashan Pathirana (http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35451v1), which formulates it as open problem 1 and resolves it with a direct proof using elementary group-theoretic and counting arguments.
solved_when: A direct, elementary proof of the group-theoretic Zhang–Yeung inequality for cardinalities of subgroups of finite groups is given, using group-theoretic and counting arguments rather than whatever indirect route was previously available.
why: It would give a clean, self-contained route to a non-Shannon-type inequality in the group-theoretic setting, paralleling how the Zhang–Yeung inequality extends Shannon's submodularity inequality in classical information theory.

title: A simple proof of the group-theoretic Zhang-Yeung inequality
open: Is there a direct, purely group-theoretic proof of the group-theoretic Zhang–Yeung inequality on subgroup cardinalities? Chan–Yeung posed giving a group-theoretic interpretation of the Zhang–Yeung inequality as an open problem, and Yeung recently pointed out again that a direct proof remains open.
solved_when: A direct proof of the inequality on subgroup cardinalities (the translated form of the Zhang–Yeung inequality stated in the source paper) is given, without passing through the entropy-theoretic original.
why: A direct group-theoretic proof would reveal the combinatorial structure underlying the entropy inequality, potentially yielding new inequalities and unifying entropy and group theory techniques.

title: A simple proof of the group-theoretic Zhang-Yeung inequality
open: Is there a short, elementary proof of the group-theoretic Zhang–Yeung inequality? The goal is to resolve this stated open problem by giving such a proof.
status: The problem was stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.35451v1 by Harold Nieuwboer and Lubashan Pathirana; no solution is recorded here.
solved_when: A short elementary proof of the group-theoretic Zhang–Yeung inequality is produced, resolving the open problem as stated in the source paper.
why: A solution supplies a simple proof of a previously open inequality in group-theoretic information theory.

title: Additive Quasi-isometry via rooted graph partitions and layering parti
open: If a graph $X$ excludes some $K$-fat minor of a fixed finite graph $H$, must $X$ be quasi-isometric to a graph with no $H$-minor at all, with the multiplicative distortion depending only on $H$? Formally: $X$ has no $K$-fat $H$ minor for some $K \in \mathbb{N}$ if and only if $X$ is $f(K)$-quasi-isometric to a graph with no $H$-minor, where $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ depends on $H$ only.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) is given, for every finite graph $H$, of the equivalence above, with an explicit function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ depending only on $H$ (or a demonstration that no such function exists).
why: It would connect the purely metric notion of fat-minor exclusion with quasi-isometric rigidity of minor-closed graph classes, allowing geometric conclusions about a graph to be drawn from the absence of a single fat forbidden minor.

title: Additive Quasi-isometry via rooted graph partitions and layering parti — question quest:add
open: For which finite graphs $H$ can forbidding a $K$-fat $H$-minor in a graph $X$, for some $K \in \mathbb{N}$, guarantee that $X$ admits a map of bounded additive distortion onto a graph with no $H$-minor at all?
solved_when: A characterization is given of the finite graphs $H$ for which, whenever $X$ has no $K$-fat $H$-minor for some $K \in \mathbb{N}$, $X$ admits a map of bounded additive distortion onto an $H$-minor-free graph.
why: It would extend quasi-isometric embedding results from excluded-minor graph classes to the weaker hypothesis of excluding only fat minors, clarifying how geometric distortion is controlled by excluded patterns.

title: Hadwiger--Nelson Problem for Typical Norms
open: Does the Hadwiger–Nelson problem — determining the chromatic number of the unit distance graph of the Euclidean norm in the plane — admit an answer for typical norms? A second sentence may sharpen: characterize the chromatic number of the unit distance graph for a generic (typical) planar norm rather than the Euclidean one.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026); see Noga Alon, Matija Bucić, James Davies, http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36220v1. The record notes that one of the key ingredients toward it is a high-dimensional, matrix generalization of the Lonely runner conjecture, which also allows the complete settlement of the view-obstruction conjecture of Schoenberg from 1978 and a more recent covering-radius conjecture of Henze and Malikiosis.
solved_when: No quantitative target is stated in the record; the natural success criterion for this problem type is a determination of the chromatic number of the unit distance graph for typical (generic) planar norms, in the sense of a measure-one or residual set of norms.
why: A solution would extend one of the most famous open problems in discrete geometry beyond the Euclidean setting, revealing which features of the Euclidean norm drive its chromatic behavior and which are shared by generic norms.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36220v1 (Noga Alon, Matija Bucić, James Davies)

title: Degree conditions for $k$-strong orientations of digraphs — conjecture conj1
open: Does every $2k$-strong digraph contain a spanning $k$-strong oriented subdigraph, for every positive integer $k$? This is conjecture conj1 of the source paper, posed in the setting of degree/strong-connectivity conditions for orientations of digraphs.
status: The conjecture was stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.36551v1 (Jørgen Bang-Jensen, Shuo Wei); no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof, for every positive integer $k$, that every $2k$-strong digraph contains a spanning $k$-strong oriented subdigraph; or a counterexample for some $k$.
why: It would establish a sharp-sounding sufficient connectivity condition guaranteeing highly strong orientations as spanning subdigraphs, advancing the program of finding degree-type conditions for $k$-strong orientations.

title: Degree conditions for $k$-strong orientations of digraphs — conjecture meynielconj
open: Does every sufficiently highly connected digraph admit a highly strong orientation under a mild degree condition? Formally, for $k \ge 1$ and $n \ge 2k+1$: does every $(2k-1)$-strong digraph $D$ on $n$ vertices with $d_D(x)+d_D(y) \ge 2n+4k-5$ for every pair of nonadjacent vertices $x,y$ admit a $k$-strong orientation?
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the statement above: every $(2k-1)$-strong digraph on $n \ge 2k+1$ vertices whose nonadjacent vertex pairs $x,y$ all satisfy $d_D(x)+d_D(y) \ge 2n+4k-5$ has a $k$-strong orientation.
why: It would extend degree-based sufficient conditions for strong orientations to the $k$-strong setting, giving a concrete handle on when high vertex-connectivity of a digraph can be preserved under orienting its arcs.

title: On the nonnegativity of monomial immanants for hook partitions — conjecture con1.1
open: For every partition of $n$ and every totally nonnegative matrix, is the corresponding monomial immanant associated with a hook partition nonnegative?
solved_when: Nonnegativity is proved (or a counterexample found) for monomial immanants of all totally nonnegative matrices and all hook partitions.
why: Nonnegative immanants generalize permanents and determinants of totally nonnegative matrices; establishing nonnegativity for hook partitions would extend classical positivity results in total positivity theory.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36665v1 (Xiangshuai Dong, Tingzeng Wu, Xing Gao)

title: Six Families of Binary Codes Arising from Ding's Conjectures — conj Conjecture 30
open: Do the six families of binary codes arising from Ding's Conjectures have the parameters conjectured in Conjecture 30? In particular, are the stated lengths, dimensions, and minimum distances (and resulting optimality properties) correct for each of the six families?
solved_when: The parameters of all six families of binary codes are rigorously determined and shown to match the conjectured values of Conjecture 30.

title: Six Families of Binary Codes Arising from Ding's Conjectures — conj Conjecture 33
open: Is Conjecture 33 of the source paper true as stated for the six families of binary codes it introduces?
solved_when: Conjecture 33 in arXiv:2609.37093v1 is proved or disproved.
why: The conjecture concerns the proposed six families of binary codes arising from Ding's conjectures; resolving it settles their claimed properties.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37093v1 (Xiaoqiang Wang, Shiyan Xiong, Mu yuan)

title: The small Davenport constant of $E_2\times C_3^r$ for $0\le r\le3$
open: What is the small Davenport constant of $E_2\times C_3^r$ for $0\le r\le3$? That is, for this family of finite groups, no formula is known for the maximal length of an indexed, product-one-free sequence, where a sequence is product-one-free if no nonempty selection of its occurrences can be ordered so that the product equals the identity.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.37262v1 (Andreas Volkmann).
solved_when: An explicit formula for the small Davenport constant of $E_2\times C_3^r$ is established for each $0\le r\le3$.
why: These small-rank cases are natural testing grounds for general results on the small Davenport constant of non-abelian and mixed groups, and settling them would clarify how the invariant behaves beyond abelian groups, where the theory is well understood.

title: Succinct Arguments for QMA in the Quantum Random Oracle Model
open: Does there exist a succinct argument system for MATH (and more broadly for QMA) in the quantum random oracle model, relying only on an idealized form of unstructured hardness and no additional cryptographic assumptions? The source paper answers this affirmatively in the oracle model, and the residual question is the extent of this feasibility result.
status: Stated as an open question in the source paper (2026), which reports that its result establishes feasibility of succinct arguments for MATH from an idealized form of unstructured hardness, without additional cryptographic assumptions, thereby answering the open question in the oracle model. Key work: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37429v2 (Alessandro Chiesa, Zihan Hu).
solved_when: A construction of succinct arguments for MATH is established from an idealized unstructured-hardness oracle alone, with no additional cryptographic assumptions — the outcome reported in the source paper.
why: It shows that succinct verification of long computations does not require structured cryptographic assumptions beyond an idealized oracle, delineating the minimal assumptions behind succinctness.

title: Products of two elements of Granville's random model in residue classe
open: Does every reduced residue class modulo M contain a product of two primes, each not exceeding M? This is the Erdős–Odlyzko–Sárközy conjecture, which remains open even under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper (2026), Banks, arXiv:2609.37434v1; it remains open even under the GRH.
solved_when: A proof (or a proof conditional on GRH) that every reduced residue class modulo M contains a product of two primes not exceeding M.
why: It would settle a long-standing conjecture on how products of small primes distribute across arithmetic progressions, a basic question in multiplicative number theory.

title: An infinite family of counterexamples to Goss's conjecture on L-functi
open: Does Goss's conjecture on L-functions hold — that is, for every "magic" index, is the "congruent to one modulo" part of the Artin L-function trivial as conjectured? This function-field analogue of Vandiver's conjecture, raised as an open problem by Anglès, remains unresolved.
status: The conjecture was stated as an open problem in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.37466v1 by David Niedbala Giraudin, following its formulation by Goss and its being raised as an open problem by Anglès. No resolution is recorded.
solved_when: The conjecture is settled: either a proof that it holds for every magic index, or an explicit counterexample (or family of counterexamples) to it.
why: It is the function-field analogue of Vandiver's conjecture, so a resolution would directly inform the arithmetic of cyclotomic extensions of function fields and the structure of their L-values.

title: The topological Bárány-Larman conjecture for prime numbers — conjecture conj:baranylarman
open: Given $d+1$ sets $X_1,\dots,X_{d+1}$, each consisting of $r$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, is there always a partition of their union into $r$ sets $C_1,\dots,C_r$ such that $|C_j \cap X_i| = 1$ for all $i,j$ and $\bigcap_{j=1}^r \operatorname{conv}(C_j) \neq \emptyset$? This is the topological Bárány–Larman conjecture, considered here for prime numbers $r$.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), extracted from a curated open-problems paper; key work: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37876v1 (Pablo Soberón).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the existence of such a partition for all positive integers $r,d$ (with $r$ prime, per the stated version) is given.
why: A solution would settle the topological analogue of the classical Bárány–Larman conjecture on colorful partitions of point sets, resolving a natural question in combinatorial geometry raised in a curated open-problems collection.

title: Improved bounds on completion of partial Latin squares — conj conj:decompo
open: Suppose $G$ is a $K_3$-divisible tripartite graph on vertex set $(V_1,V_2,V_3)$ with $|V_1|=|V_2|=|V_3|=n$, where $n$ is sufficiently large. Can $G$ be decomposed into edge-disjoint triangles — and if so, with what divisibility or degree conditions guaranteeing this?
solved_when: A theorem (or counterexample) resolving whether every $K_3$-divisible tripartite graph with equal parts of size $n$, for all sufficiently large $n$, admits a triangle decomposition; quantitative thresholds on $n$ and any degree conditions should be stated explicitly.
why: A resolution would yield improved bounds for the completion of partial Latin squares, since a triangle decomposition of the associated tripartite graph corresponds exactly to completing the square.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37877v1 (Jack Allsop, Candida Bowtell, Thomas Lesgourgues)

title: Smyth's Conjecture on the Mahler Measure of non-reciprocal trinomials — conjecture conj:1.1
open: What is the smallest limit point of the Mahler measure $M(P)$ as $P$ ranges over non-reciprocal polynomials $P(z)$? More precisely, Smyth's conjecture proposes a specific value for this smallest limit point within the class of non-reciprocal trinomials.
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper (2026); see Paul M Voutier, http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37886v1.
solved_when: The conjectured value for the smallest limit point of the Mahler measure of non-reciprocal polynomials is established, or refuted by an explicit counterexample.
why: Determining the limit points of Mahler measures clarifies the fine structure of the spectrum of values that measures of non-reciprocal polynomials can attain, which is central to Lehmer-type problems.

title: Towards verifiable quantum advantage with random circuits: Observables
open: Is the \(n^{-1/2}\) scaling obtained for \(\mathrm{OTOC}^{(1)}\) in one dimension actually tight, or can it be improved? Formally, the question asks whether the bound on this out-of-time-order correlator observable for random circuits in one dimension is optimal in its dependence on the system size \(n\).
solved_when: A proof that the \(n^{-1/2}\) scaling of \(\mathrm{OTOC}^{(1)}\) in one dimension is tight, or a construction/analysis achieving a strictly better scaling.
why: Tightness of this scaling determines whether random-circuit observables can genuinely support verifiable quantum advantage at this scaling, or whether the claimed behavior is an artifact of a loose bound.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37890v1 (Antonio A. Mele, Francesco A. Mele, Jarrod R. McClean)

title: Can We Break Fine-Grained and NP-Hardness Barriers if We've Seen the G
open: Do the games considered in this paper admit polynomial-time algorithms, or are they provably hard? This is the question of settling the exact computational complexity of these games.
status: The source paper (arXiv 2026) states this as a prominent open question; no algorithm or hardness result is known. Key work: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37979v1 (Dani Dorfman, Simon Döring, Martin G. Herold).
solved_when: For each of the games in question, either a polynomial-time algorithm is given or a hardness proof (fine-grained or NP-hardness) is established.
why: A polynomial-time algorithm would break the perceived fine-grained and NP-hardness barriers for these games, while hardness proofs would confirm those barriers as genuine.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37979v1 (Dani Dorfman, Simon Döring, Martin G. Herold)

title: Resource Compatibility in Optimal Quantum Symmetry Testing
open: For the qutrit Clifford group, do Wigner-positive optimal protocols for symmetry testing exist beyond nine queries? Such protocols are known to exist at three and four queries, and to fail between five and nine, leaving the high-query regime unsettled.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.38134v1 (Yimeng Cao, Ranyiliu Chen, Chengkai Zhu); Wigner-positive optimal protocols exist at three and four queries but not from five through nine queries.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that Wigner-positive optimal protocols exist for the qutrit Clifford group at some query count greater than nine, or a proof that none exist there.
why: It determines whether positivity constraints in phase-space formulations are a genuine obstruction to optimality in symmetry testing, or only a low-query artifact.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38134v1 (Yimeng Cao, Ranyiliu Chen, Chengkai Zhu)

title: A nearly linear bound for the Lovász conjecture
open: Does every connected graph have a vertex set of bounded absolute size — a constant number of vertices — that meets every longest path? Walther answered the original Lovász conjecture in the negative in 1969, so the question is whether a nearly linear (indeed constant) bound can still be achieved.
status: Walther answered the original conjecture negatively in 1969. The problem is stated as open in the source paper, Bowen Li and Abhishek Methuku, arXiv:2609.38135v1 (2026).
solved_when: A proof that some absolute constant k exists such that every connected graph has a set of at most k vertices intersecting every longest path (or, failing that, a nearly linear bound replacing "constant" with an explicit sublinear function).
why: It settles the surviving quantitative core of the Lovász conjecture after Walther's negative answer, determining whether hitting all longest paths is a genuinely bounded-size task in every graph.

title: The Bias Conjecture for One-Parameter, Non-Isotrivial Elliptic Curve F
open: In the second moment of the one-parameter, non-isotrivial elliptic curve family, does the dominant negative-bias term predicted by the bias conjecture actually exist? Formally, writing $_{w,p}$ for the coefficient of $p^{w/2}$ in the cohomological decomposition of the second moment, the conjecture asserts that for the largest $w<4$ where $_{w,p}$ does not average to $0$, it averages to less than $0$ over the primes.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, for the largest $w<4$ with $_{w,p}$ not averaging to zero over primes, the average of $_{w,p}$ over the primes is strictly negative.
why: It verifies that the secondary terms in the second moment of this family genuinely bias downward, sharpening our understanding of how arithmetic invariants of elliptic curve families deviate from their main-term asymptotics.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38664v1 (Lucas Chen, Joshua Im, Steven J. Miller)

title: Quantum Time-Lock Puzzles in the Quantum Random Oracle Model
open: Can time-lock puzzles be constructed from symmetric-key assumptions alone? More precisely, we lack a construction of timed-release puzzles whose security rests purely on symmetric-key primitives rather than structured algebraic assumptions.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.38894v1 (Prabhanjan Ananth, Yao-Ting Lin).
solved_when: A construction of time-lock puzzles is given whose security is proven using only symmetric-key assumptions, with no additional structural assumptions invoked.
why: Time-lock puzzles currently depend on structured assumptions; a symmetric-key-only construction would extend this cryptographic tool to settings where only symmetric primitives are available or trusted.

title: Complete bipartite embeddings, lattice non-embeddability, and non-Eucl
open: Does every finite complete bipartite graph admit a scale-embedding, in both the string and the sequence versions of the notion?
status: Stated as Open Problem 37 in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.38919v1 (Fengqi Hou); no resolution is recorded in the census.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) that every finite complete bipartite graph scale-embeds, covering both the string version and the sequence version.
why: It would complete the embeddability picture for complete bipartite graphs, the basic building blocks of bipartite graph theory, within the scale-embedding framework introduced in the source paper.

title: Optimal learning of covariant quantum states and channels
open: What is the optimal query complexity for learning a permutation-covariant channel to a general target diamond-distance error? The matching lower bound is currently known only for sufficiently small fixed error, leaving the general-error regime undetermined.
solved_when: A matching lower bound on the diamond-distance error is established for arbitrary target error, pinning down the optimal query complexity of learning the permutation-covariant channel at all error levels.
why: It completes the characterization of optimal covariant channel learning, so that sample-efficient protocols like the Hayashi measurement circuit can be shown (or shown not) to be information-theoretically optimal across all error regimes.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39280v1 (Satoshi Yoshida, Kazuki Okigami, Pietro M. Posta)

title: Non-finite Axiomatizability and Undecidability of $\mathsf{Cheq}$
open: Is the theory MATH finitely axiomatizable — that is, can all of its theorems be derived from a single finite set of axioms?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.39577v1 (Han Xiao), which notes it is a longstanding open problem.
solved_when: A proof that MATH is finitely axiomatizable (exhibiting a finite axiomatization) or a proof that no finite axiomatization exists.
why: Finite axiomatizability would reduce reasoning about all of mathematics to a fixed finite basis, with consequences for formalization and decidability questions; failure would show mathematics is essentially irreducibly infinite in its foundations.

title: QMA(2) with Limited Shared Entanglement
open: Are two unentangled quantum witnesses more powerful than a single one? Formally, does QMA(2) strictly contain QMA?
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that QMA(2) ≠ QMA.
why: It would settle whether entanglement across witnesses genuinely adds verification power, a basic structural question in quantum complexity theory.

title: Verifiable quantum advantage based on polynomials with planted structu
open: Given a cubic Boolean polynomial $g$ and an integer $h$, decide whether $g$ has an independent space of dimension at least $h$.
solved_when: An algorithm (classical or quantum) is given that decides, for arbitrary cubic Boolean polynomials $g$ and integers $h$, whether an independent space of dimension at least $h$ exists, together with a proof of its correctness.
why: The problem arises as an open question in a curated set of problems on verifiable quantum advantage based on polynomials with planted structure; resolving it would clarify the computational complexity landscape underpinning that proposal.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39918v1 (Markus Bläser, Michael Gullans, Dominik Hangleiter)

title: Verifiable quantum advantage based on polynomials with planted structu
open: Given a cubic Boolean polynomial $g$ with an independent space $V$ of dimension $h$, recover the planted independent space $V$ itself, rather than merely detecting its existence.
solved_when: An algorithm (classical or quantum) that, given $g$ and $h$, outputs the space $V$ of dimension $h$ is provided and analyzed.
why: Finding the planted structure is the natural search analogue of the detection task; resolving it determines whether the planted-structure scheme can support verifiable quantum advantage.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39918v1 (Markus Bläser, Michael Gullans, Dominik Hangleiter)

title: Haah's 3D cubic code thermalizes rapidly
open: Is Haah's 3D cubic code a self-correcting quantum memory? More formally, does the code's stored quantum information remain protected at finite temperature for a time that grows with system size, without active error correction?
status: The question is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.39959v1 (Sebastian Stengele, Libor Caha, Ángela Capel).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the 3D cubic code is self-correcting — specifically, a demonstration of whether quantum information persists at nonzero temperature for a lifetime increasing with the system size.
why: Self-correcting quantum memories would allow quantum storage without continuous active error correction, and the cubic code is a leading candidate where fracton structure might make this possible.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39959v1 (Sebastian Stengele, Libor Caha, Ángela Capel)

title: Logarithmic-Depth Fermion Sampling: Anticoncentration and Average-Case
open: Is it hard to sample the output distribution of logarithmic-depth fermionic circuits to within constant total-variation distance of the true distribution? A formal version asks whether no efficient classical sampler can achieve constant total-variation distance for this family.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.40100v1 (Natansh Mathur, Iordanis Kerenidis).
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of hardness of sampling logarithmic-depth fermion sampling within constant total-variation distance is given, including the anticoncentration and average-case components the record indicates.
why: It would extend quantum-supremacy-style hardness evidence to shallower fermionic circuit classes, clarifying which depths of fermion sampling remain classically intractable.

title: Improved Quantum Query Bounds for Boolean Matrix Product Verification
open: What is the true quantum query complexity of verifying a Boolean matrix product? Concretely, can the gap between the known \(n^{5/4}\) lower bound and \(O(n^{17/12})\) upper bound for Boolean Matrix Product Verification be closed?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40180v2 (Amin Shiraz Gilani, François Le Gall, Xingyu Zhou), which gives the \(n^{5/4}\) lower bound and \(O(n^{17/12})\) upper bound.
solved_when: Matching quantum query bounds for Boolean Matrix Product Verification are established — that is, the gap between the \(n^{5/4}\) lower bound and the \(O(n^{17/12})\) upper bound is resolved (either by an improved algorithm or a stronger lower bound meeting the other side).
why: Closing the gap pins down the exact quantum query complexity of a fundamental verification task, sharpening our understanding of the quantum advantage over classical verification for matrix multiplication.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40180v2 (Amin Shiraz Gilani, François Le Gall, Xingyu Zhou)

title: Superlinear Quantum Query Lower Bounds for Subgraph Detection
open: Do there exist unconditional superlinear lower bounds on the bounded-error quantum query complexity of subgraph detection? More precisely, can one prove such bounds unconditionally for this problem class?
status: Stated as an open question in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.40263v2 (Amin Shiraz Gilani, Xingyu Zhou); the paper's stated open question 1 concerns proving the first unconditional superlinear lower bounds for this problem.
solved_when: An unconditional superlinear lower bound on the bounded-error quantum query complexity of subgraph detection is established.
why: Such bounds would settle how much quantum speedup subgraph detection admits, giving a baseline against which all quantum algorithms for the problem must be measured.

title: Quantum Fine-Grained Lower Bounds for SetDisjointness via Sub-Linear R
open: Can the 3SUM problem be solved in truly subquadratic classical time, or does every algorithm require essentially quadratic time? Formally, the conjecture asserts that 3SUM admits no classical algorithm running in $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ time for any constant $\varepsilon > 0$.
status: The conjecture was stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.40293v1 (Jeremy Huang, Young Kun Ko, Chunhao Wang).
solved_when: A proof that no classical algorithm solves 3SUM in $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ time for any constant $\varepsilon > 0$ resolves the conjecture in the affirmative; a deterministic algorithm achieving such a bound refutes it.
why: The conjecture is a cornerstone of fine-grained complexity: it underpins quadratic-condition lower bounds for many seemingly unrelated problems, so resolving it either secures or collapses a large web of conditional hardness results.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40293v1 (Jeremy Huang, Young Kun Ko, Chunhao Wang)

title: More mutually unbiased bases
open: How many mutually unbiased bases can exist in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space whose dimension is not a power of a prime? That is, the maximal number of mutually unbiased bases remains unknown in such dimensions.
solved_when: The maximal number of mutually unbiased bases is determined (exactly, or by a matching construction and upper bound) in at least one composite dimension that is not a prime power.
why: The prime-power case is well understood, so these remaining dimensions are the main gap in the classification; settling any one would resolve a long-standing basic question in quantum information geometry.

title: More mutually unbiased bases
open: Do four mutually unbiased bases exist in dimension six? This is a leading open question in quantum information science, since dimension six is the smallest composite dimension where standard constructions fail.
status: Stated as an open problem in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.40311v1 (Mateo Cárdenes Wuttig, Joseph Tindall).
solved_when: An explicit construction of four MUBs in dimension six is given, or the existence of a fourth MUB is ruled out.
why: Dimension six is the smallest case where the maximum number of MUBs is unknown; settling it would resolve whether complete sets of MUBs can exist outside prime-power dimensions, with direct consequences for quantum tomography and cryptography.

title: Singularity of harmonic measures for hyperbolic lattices
open: Does the harmonic measure associated to a hyperbolic lattice remain singular in higher dimensions? This is open in particular for arithmetic lattices of the second type in odd dimensions at least five and for the exceptional trialitarian arithmetic lattices in dimension seven; see Bregman--Incerti-Medici.
solved_when: Singularity of the harmonic measure is established (or refuted) for arithmetic lattices of the second type in odd dimensions at least five and for the exceptional trialitarian arithmetic lattices in dimension seven.
why: It would complete the singularity picture for harmonic measures of hyperbolic lattices across all arithmetic types and dimensions, where the higher-dimensional cases remain unresolved.

title: Global Well-Posedness of the Kuramoto--Sivashinsky Equation in One and
open: Does the unconstrained two-dimensional Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation admit global well-posedness for strong solutions in general? The constrained version admits such a result, but the unconstrained case remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of global well-posedness of strong solutions for the unconstrained two-dimensional Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation in general.
why: Resolving the unconstrained case would complete the well-posedness picture for the two-dimensional KS equation, removing the gap between the constrained and unconstrained theories.

title: Global Well-Posedness of the Kuramoto--Sivashinsky Equation in One and
open: Is the standard multidimensional Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation globally well posed? Despite the progress to date, general global well-posedness remains open for \(d \ge 2\), both in the periodic setting and in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of global well-posedness of the standard KS equation is established in dimensions \(d \ge 2\), in both the periodic setting and \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
why: Settling this would complete the foundational analytic picture for one of the basic models of pattern formation and front propagation, closing the gap between the well-understood one-dimensional theory and higher dimensions.

title: Global Well-Posedness of the Kuramoto--Sivashinsky Equation in One and
open: Does the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation, posed without constraints in two and three spatial dimensions, admit a global well-posedness theory? That is, can one establish existence, uniqueness, and continuous dependence on data for all time in 2D and 3D?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026): Harsh Tiwari, Manil T. Mohan, arXiv:2610.00248v1 (http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00248v1).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of global well-posedness — global-in-time existence, uniqueness, and stability of solutions — for the unconstrained Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation in both two and three spatial dimensions.
why: Global well-posedness in 2D and 3D is the foundational regularity question for this equation, and its resolution would underpin any further analysis of attractors, long-time dynamics, or control in higher dimensions.

title: Global Well-Posedness of the Kuramoto--Sivashinsky Equation in One and
open: Is the two-dimensional Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation globally well-posed? That is, can existence, uniqueness, and continuous dependence on data be established for all time in the two-dimensional setting?
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of global well-posedness for the two-dimensional Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation is given, removing the "constrained setting" restriction under which only a partial resolution currently exists.
why: A full resolution would settle one of the well-known foundational questions for the KS equation, and currently results hold only under constraints, leaving the core dynamics of the two-dimensional problem unresolved.

title: Quantum Secret Sharing and Error Correction vs No-Cloning — conjecture conj
open: Does an $((n,,k))$ quantum secret sharing scheme exist exactly when the associated access structure graph is $k$-colorable? A formal statement of the conjecture: such a QSS scheme exists if and only if the access structure graph admits a proper $k$-coloring.
solved_when: The equivalence is proven (or refuted by counterexample): a $((n,,k))$-QSS scheme exists if and only if the associated access structure graph is $k$-colorable.
why: It would tie the existence of quantum secret sharing schemes directly to a classical graph-coloring property, giving a combinatorial criterion for when quantum secrets can be shared subject to no-cloning constraints.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00441v1 (Steven Chien, Ishani Mukherjee, Mark Zhandry)

title: Clifford-hierarchy stabilizer formalism with applications to twisted q — conjecture conj:intro_level_k
open: For a TQD topological order ${D}^({Z}_p^n)$, what is the minimum level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy needed to realize a stabilizer code whose codestate lies in the ${D}^({Z}_p^n)$ phase? Formally, the conjecture asserts that this minimum $k$ is given by a specific closed-form expression in $p$ and $n$.
solved_when: The conjecture conj:intro_level_k is proved or refuted: a proof establishes the stated formula for the minimum $k$ for every TQD topological order ${D}^({Z}_p^n)$, or a counterexample exhibits a phase where the minimum differs.

title: Clifford-hierarchy stabilizer formalism with applications to twisted q
open: Can every locality-preserving unitary gate that is compatible with a level-$k$ Clifford-hierarchy code in $d$ spatial dimensions be placed no higher than level $d+k-1$ of the Clifford hierarchy? In other words, does locality preservation force an upper bound on the hierarchy level of such gates?
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2610.00464v1 (Christopher Fechisin, Kieran Cooney, Mathi Raja); no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given, for general $d$ and $k$, that any locality-preserving unitary preserving a level-$k$ code must lie in level at most $d+k-1$ of the Clifford hierarchy.
why: Such a bound would sharply characterize which transversal-like gates fault-tolerant level-$k$ codes can support in $d$ dimensions, constraining code design for quantum computation; without it, the reach of locality-preserving gates on hierarchy codes remains unbounded in principle.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00464v1 (Christopher Fechisin, Kieran Cooney, Mathi Raja)

title: Blind Unforgeability implies Plus-One Unforgeability
open: Does quantum blind-unforgeability of a blind signature scheme imply quantum plus-one unforgeability? The source paper states this as an open question, asking formally whether every scheme secure in the blind-unforgeability sense is also secure against the stronger plus-one adversary.
status: The question is stated as open in the source paper (2026), which proves that quantum blind-unforgeability implies quantum plus-one unforgeability, thereby settling an open question in the literature. Key work: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00517v1 (Mehil Agarwal, Calliope S. Reimann, Fang Song).
solved_when: A proof (or a separating counterexample) resolving the implication from quantum blind-unforgeability to quantum plus-one unforgeability is given, as posed in the source paper.
why: It would complete the security-hierarchy picture for blind signature unforgeability notions in the quantum setting, clarifying which security definition schemes must target.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00517v1 (Mehil Agarwal, Calliope S. Reimann, Fang Song)

title: Negative Correlations for Forests and the $q<1$ Random Cluster Model — conj conj:sumsofsquares
open: Does the Rayleigh difference of the spanning-tree polynomial of a finite graph decompose as a sum of monomials in the edge weights times squares of polynomials in those weights? Formally, for a finite graph $G=(V,E)$ and distinct edges $e,f \in E$, can $\mathcal{R}_{ef}(\tau_G)$ be written as a finite sum of monomials in the edge weights multiplied by squares of polynomials in those weights, in the more precise combinatorial formulation of Wagner?
solved_when: An identity is proved expressing the Rayleigh difference $\mathcal{R}_{ef}(\tau_G)$ for arbitrary finite graphs $G$ as a finite sum of monomial-in-edge-weights times squares-of-polynomial terms, or a counterexample is exhibited.
why: Such a sum-of-squares identity would yield the negative-correlation (Rayleigh) property for forests, connecting to the long-standing negative association question for the $q<1$ random cluster model.

title: Negative Correlations for Forests and the $q<1$ Random Cluster Model — conj conj:grimmett-winkler
open: Let $0<q<1$ and let all edge weights be nonnegative. Then, for every finite graph $G$ and distinct edges $e,f$ — a negative-correlation statement for the random cluster model with $q<1$ (and, per the title, for forests) is asserted to hold.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) of the stated correlation inequality is given for every finite graph $G$, all distinct edges $e,f$, all nonnegative edge weights, and all $0<q<1$.
why: Negative correlation for the $q<1$ random cluster model is a foundational structural question; establishing it would unlock sharp probabilistic controls in a regime where the standard positive-association tools of the $q\geq1$ case fail.

title: Negative Correlations for Forests and the $q<1$ Random Cluster Model
open: Does negative correlation hold for forests and for the random cluster model in the regime $q<1$, in full generality? A precise formulation would establish the expected negative-correlation inequalities for these measures in complete generality, beyond the special cases currently known.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2610.00549v1 (Recep Altar Çiçeksiz, Mohan Ravichandran).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the negative correlation conjecture for forests and the $q<1$ random cluster model in full generality is given.
why: Negative correlation underlies the toolboxes used to analyze these models; establishing it in full generality would complete a basic structural picture that is currently only available in special cases.

title: Optimal two-mode bosonic loss codes from finite group symmetry — conjecture binary-polyhedral-conjecture
open: Does every integer $d \geq 2$ admit a rank-two bosonic loss code of distance at least $d$ built from finite group symmetry? Formally, the conjecture asserts that such a code exists at $n_d = (3d^2+1)/4$, with $2O$ (binary octahedral) symmetry for even $d$ and $2T$ (binary tetrahedral) symmetry for odd $d$.
solved_when: A construction (or proof of existence) is given of a rank-two loss code of distance at least $d$ at $n_d = (3d^2+1)/4$ for every integer $d \geq 2$, with the stated $2O$ symmetry for even $d$ and $2T$ symmetry for odd $d$.
why: It would establish optimality of two-mode bosonic loss codes through finite group symmetry, giving a systematic family of codes rather than ad hoc constructions for quantum communication against loss.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00561v1 (Argyris Giannisis Manes, Mahadevan Subramanian, Liang Jiang)

title: Beyond odd characteristic: Faster isomorphism testing of 2-groups of F — problem def:tensor_iso
open: Given two alternating 3-tensors $T$ and $T'$ of dimension $m \times n \times n$ over some field $\mathbb{F}$, are there matrices $M \in \mathrm{GL}(m, \mathbb{F})$ and $N \in \mathrm{GL}(n, \mathbb{F})$ such that $T^{\mathrm{Trans}(M, N)} = T'$? In other words, is there an efficient algorithm to decide isomorphism of such tensors under this transvection-type action?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), Joshua A. Grochow, Gábor Ivanyos, Youming Qiao, http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00874v1.
solved_when: An algorithm is given that decides, for two alternating 3-tensors of dimension $m \times n \times n$ over a field $\mathbb{F}$, whether some $M \in \mathrm{GL}(m, \mathbb{F})$ and $N \in \mathrm{GL}(n, \mathbb{F})$ satisfy $T^{\mathrm{Trans}(M, N)} = T'$, with a running time faster than the state of the art (no quantitative target is stated in the record).
why: This is the tensor-isomorphism obstruction at the heart of faster isomorphism testing for 2-groups of Frattini class 2; settling it would push those group-isomorphism algorithms beyond odd characteristic.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00874v1 (Joshua A. Grochow, Gábor Ivanyos, Youming Qiao)

title: Perfect matching covers of claw-free cubic graphs — conjecture conj:bf
open: Does every bridgeless cubic graph admit six perfect matchings with the property that each edge lies in exactly two of them?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the statement that every bridgeless cubic graph has six perfect matchings covering every edge exactly twice.
why: It would settle a concrete covering conjecture for cubic graphs, refining how perfect matchings can uniformly cover bridgeless cubic graphs.

title: Perfect matching covers of claw-free cubic graphs — conjecture conj:berge
open: Can every bridgeless cubic graph have its edge set covered by five perfect matchings? Formally, does every such graph admit a family of five perfect matchings whose union contains all edges?
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit counterexample) that the edge set of every bridgeless cubic graph is contained in the union of five perfect matchings.
why: It would settle the conjecture conj:berge on perfect matching covers, a natural structural limit on how few perfect matchings suffice in cubic graphs.

title: Perfect matching covers of claw-free cubic graphs — conjecture conj:5cdc
open: Does every bridgeless graph admit a family of five even subgraphs in which each edge lies in exactly two of them?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2610.01137v1 (Huaibin Zhou, Xiumei Wang); no partial results are recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit counterexample) that every bridgeless graph has five even subgraphs covering each edge exactly twice.
why: This is a bounded analogue of the classical circuit-decomposition problems; settling it would sharpen our understanding of how even subgraphs can be combined to cover bridgeless graphs uniformly.

title: Morley Simplices in Higher Dimensions: Regularity, Reflections, and Co — conjecture ld:two-reflections
open: Is it true that whenever the Morley simplex of an $n$-simplex is regular, with $n \in \{4,5\}$, the original simplex must admit two hyperplane reflection symmetries, each interchanging a disjoint pair of vertices?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that, for each $n \in \{4,5\}$, regularity of the Morley simplex of an $n$-simplex implies the existence of two hyperplane reflection symmetries of the simplex interchanging disjoint pairs of vertices.
why: It would extend the Morley-simplex regularity phenomenon to higher dimensions and tie it directly to reflection symmetry, clarifying how rigid the Morley construction is beyond the classical triangle case.

title: Unbounded separation between definite and indefinite causal order in f
open: Can quantum metrology with an indefinite causal order achieve an unbounded advantage over any strategy with definite causal order, using only finite-dimensional systems? Put formally, is there a finite-dimensional metrological task where the indefinite-causal-order (ICO) advantage over definite causal order (DCO) grows without bound?
solved_when: A family of finite-dimensional metrological tasks is exhibited for which the ratio of the ICO performance (e.g., precision or information gain) to the best DCO strategy is unbounded, together with a proof that no finite-dimensional DCO strategy can match it.
why: It would establish indefinite causal order as a genuine, unbounded resource for quantum metrology rather than a curiosity, clarifying the ultimate advantage of causal non-classicality in information-processing tasks.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01462v1 (Yanglin Hu, Zi-Shen Li, Giulio Chiribella)

title: $K$-$k$-Schur functions are $k$-Schur positive — conjecture conj:BMS
open: Are the $K$-$k$-Schur functions positive sums of $k$-Schur functions? A formulation of this positivity (conjecture conj:BMS from paper 2610.01708) asks for a $k$-Schur-positive expansion of the $K$-$k$-Schur basis.
solved_when: An explicit (or provably existing) expansion of each $K$-$k$-Schur function as a nonnegative integer combination of $k$-Schur functions is given; the record states no further quantitative targets.

title: Square products of factorials and a conjecture of Erdős and Graham
open: Do the natural densities $\lim_{X\to\infty} D_k(X)/X$ exist for $k = 4, 5, 6$, and if so, can their values be written down explicitly as Euler products or convergent series?
solved_when: For each of $k = 4, 5, 6$, the existence of the limit $D_k(X)/X$ is proved and its value is given by an explicit Euler product or convergent series.
why: These densities quantify how often products of $k$ factorials are perfect squares, extending the numerical/analytic picture behind the Erdős–Graham conjecture on square products of factorials.

title: Improved upper bounds on the list chromatic number of $K_t$-minor-free — conjecture conj:list-linear
open: Is there an absolute constant $C$ such that every $K_t$-minor-free graph has list chromatic number at most $Ct$? More precisely, does the conjecture conj:list-linear hold, giving a linear-in-$t$ upper bound on the choice number of $K_t$-minor-free graphs?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2610.01946v1 (Yangyan Gu, Rongxing Xu); no improved bound or partial resolution is recorded in the census.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the existence of an absolute constant $C$ with $\chi_\ell(G) \le Ct$ for every $K_t$-minor-free graph $G$; no specific value of $C$ is demanded beyond absoluteness.
why: It would establish that sparsity in the minor sense forces list-colorability to grow only linearly in the excluded clique size, resolving the natural analogue of Hadwiger-type coloring questions in the list setting.

title: Linear arboricity conjecture for infinite graphs — conjecture conj2
open: Can every partial edge-coloring of $K_{2n+1}$ whose color classes are linear forests be completed into a Hamiltonian decomposition? Specifically, if $H$ is a subgraph of $K_{2n+1}$ with $n$ edges whose edges are colored so that every color class induces a linear forest, does this coloring extend to an edge-coloring of $K_{2n+1}$ with $n$ colors in which every color class induces a Hamilton cycle?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that every such partial coloring of a subgraph $H \subseteq K_{2n+1}$ with $n$ edges and linear-forest color classes extends to a decomposition of $K_{2n+1}$ into $n$ Hamilton cycles.
why: It would establish an extension/completion form of the linear arboricity and Hamiltonian decomposition questions for complete graphs of odd order, showing that partial linear-forest colorings never obstruct a full Hamiltonian decomposition.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02065v1 (Leandro Aurichi, Rodrigo Santos Monteiro, Caio Fernando Rodrigues)

title: Linear arboricity conjecture for infinite graphs
open: Does every connected infinite cubic graph admit a decomposition of its edge set into two isomorphic linear forests? In other words, can the edges be split into two disjoint linear forests — forests whose components are all paths — that are isomorphic to each other?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that every connected infinite cubic graph has an edge decomposition into two isomorphic linear forests.
why: It extends the linear arboricity conjecture to infinite graphs with a symmetry twist, and a positive answer would give a clean structural decomposition theorem for infinite cubic graphs.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02065v1 (Leandro Aurichi, Rodrigo Santos Monteiro, Caio Fernando Rodrigues)

title: Typical intersecting families at $n=2k+1$ and $n=2k+2$ — conjecture conj:BGLW1
open: For every $n \ge 2k+2$, are almost all intersecting families in $\binom{[n]}{k}$ trivial? More precisely, as $k \to \infty$, is the number of intersecting families dominated by the trivial (star) ones?
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that for every $n \ge 2k+2$, almost all intersecting families in $\binom{[n]}{k}$ are trivial as $k \to \infty$, resolving conjecture conj:BGLW1.
why: It would complete the enumeration of typical intersecting families at and beyond the boundary cases $n = 2k+1$ and $n = 2k+2$, settling when triviality becomes the generic behavior.

title: Proving at Scale for Universal Algebra
open: Is the finite basis problem decidable for semigroups? The finite basis problem — deciding whether a given algebraic structure has a finite equational basis — is undecidable in general in universal algebra, yet the semigroup case remains open.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), a curated open-problems paper by João Araújo, Jan Hůla, and Mikoláš Janota (http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02500v2); it is undecidable in general, with the semigroup case remaining open.
solved_when: An answer is given to whether every finite semigroup (or equivalently, a decision procedure exists for whether a given finite semigroup) has a finite basis of identities — resolving decidability of the finite basis problem for semigroups.
why: A resolution would settle one of the most longstanding open questions in universal algebra, determining whether finite semigroups behave like the general undecidable setting or admit a decidable finite basis criterion.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02500v2 (João Araújo, Jan Hůla, Mikoláš Janota)

title: Positive discrepancy of graphs far from Turán graphs — conj c2
open: Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Must every regular $n$-vertex graph that is $\varepsilon$-far from every Turán graph have second largest eigenvalue at least $cn^{1/4}$, for some constant $c > 0$? Formally, there exists $c>0$ such that if $G$ is a regular $n$-vertex graph that is $\varepsilon$-far from every Turán graph, then its second largest eigenvalue is at least $cn^{1/4}$.
solved_when: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ a constant $c > 0$ is exhibited such that every regular $n$-vertex graph that is $\varepsilon$-far from every Turán graph has second largest eigenvalue at least $cn^{1/4}$, or a counterexample is constructed.
why: It would quantify how strong spectral expansion must be for regular graphs that are far from Turán graphs, connecting eigenvalue bounds to graph discrepancy.

title: Continual Graph Memory for Mathematical Research Agents
open: A matching growth estimate remains open. {302.} Let \(f(N)\) be the largest size of a subset of \(\{1, ,N\}\) containing no distinct \(a,b,c\) with \(1/a=1/b+1/c\)~.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02945v1 (Junyi Zhang, Jinxi Yu, Eric Hanchen Jiang)

title: A note on partitioning the vertex set of a graph into a dominating set — problem problem:disjoint-DLD
open: Can the vertex set of every isolate-free graph be partitioned into a dominating set and a locating dominating set?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03131v1 (Dipayan Chakraborty, Florent Foucaud, Michael A. Henning); no further progress is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or a counterexample) resolving, for every isolate-free graph, whether its vertex set partitions into a dominating set and a locating dominating set.
why: It would settle a natural structural question about the coexistence of domination and location-detection in graphs, posed in a curated open-problems collection.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03131v1 (Dipayan Chakraborty, Florent Foucaud, Michael A. Henning)

title: Classical Algorithms for Bipartite Quantum Max-Cut on Dense Expanders
open: Does the Bipartite Quantum Max-Cut problem on dense expanders admit a polynomial-time classical randomized algorithm — that is, does the problem lie in BPP? A second sentence sharpening it formally: the question is whether randomness alone (without quantum computation) suffices to solve it exactly or to the achieved approximation level in polynomial time on a classical machine.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026) by Stuart Wayland, Zackary Jorquera, and Alexandra Kolla (arXiv:2610.03670v1).
solved_when: A polynomial-time classical randomized algorithm for the problem is exhibited (placing it in BPP), or the problem is shown not to lie in BPP.
why: A positive answer would remove any need for quantum hardware for this problem class, showing classical randomized computation captures it; a negative answer would provide evidence that quantum computation genuinely offers an advantage here.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03670v1 (Stuart Wayland, Zackary Jorquera, Alexandra Kolla)

title: Classical Algorithms for Bipartite Quantum Max-Cut on Dense Expanders
open: What is the classical computational complexity of the Quantum Max-Cut problem restricted to bipartite instances? Formally, is there an efficient classical algorithm for the bipartite case, or is it hard — a question that remains open despite Quantum Max-Cut being a well-studied local Hamiltonian problem?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2610.03670v1 (Zackary Jorquera, Alexandra Kolla, Stuart Wayland), which notes that Quantum Max-Cut is well-studied but the classical complexity of the bipartite case remains open.
solved_when: A resolution of the classical complexity of the bipartite case of Quantum Max-Cut: either a polynomial-time classical algorithm deciding/approximating it, or a proof of classical hardness.
why: Bipartite graphs are the natural structured special case of this local Hamiltonian problem, and settling their complexity would clarify how far classical computation can go on Quantum Max-Cut before genuinely quantum resources are needed.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03670v1 (Stuart Wayland, Zackary Jorquera, Alexandra Kolla)

title: Uniform meandric systems as percolation on planar maps: conjectures an — conjecture conj-a
open: Does a meandric-system analogue of the RSW-type crossing bound hold — namely, for every $n \geq 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{Z}+1/2$, given a box $B_n(x)$ and a uniform open meandric system, is the probability that there exists both a top-left to bottom-right green crossing and a bottom-left to top-right green crossing at most $1/4$?
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the bound: for every $n \geq 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{Z}+1/2$, in a box $B_n(x)$ under a uniform open meandric system, the probability of both a top-left to bottom-right green crossing and a bottom-left to top-right green crossing is at most $1/4$.
why: Such a crossing-probability bound is the standard entry point to RSW-type arguments, and would control dependence in the percolation-on-planar-maps representation of uniform meandric systems.

title: Uniform meandric systems as percolation on planar maps: conjectures an — conjecture conj-b
open: In a uniform open meandric system, is it true that inside the box $B_n(x)$ with $x \in \mathbb{Z} + 1/2$, green crossings become asymptotically impossible in the sense that one cannot have both a top-left to bottom-right green crossing and a bottom-left to top-right green crossing? Formally, the probability that both such crossings exist decreases monotonically to zero as $n$ tends to infinity.
solved_when: It is proved that the probability of the simultaneous existence of a top-left to bottom-right green crossing and a bottom-left to top-right green crossing in $B_n(x)$ (with $x \in \mathbb{Z} + 1/2$) under a uniform open meandric system decreases monotonically to zero as $n \to \infty$.
why: Resolving it would clarify whether uniform meandric systems behave like a critical or subcritical percolation model on planar maps, a key step toward understanding their scaling limits.

title: A linear-in-$q$ range of dimensions for the MDS conjecture over $\math
open: Is the MDS conjecture true over proper extension fields in the full range of dimensions? It is known over prime fields, but the general case over proper extension fields remains unresolved.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2610.03740v2 (Xiang Fan); the conjecture is known over prime fields, and a survey of the area is referenced there, but no general result over proper extension fields is recorded.
solved_when: The MDS conjecture is proved (or disproved) over proper extension fields for all dimensions in the conjectured range.
why: Extending the conjecture from prime fields to proper extension fields would complete the MDS conjecture in its natural generality, settling the fundamental limits on the length of MDS codes.

title: Upper $k$-Star-Forming Sets, $k$-Independence, and Upper Domination — problem prob:sf2complexity
open: What is the computational complexity of computing $SF_2(G)$ on bipartite graphs? Formally, this asks for the complexity of deciding, given a bipartite graph $G$ and an integer $t$, whether $G$ has a minimal $2$-star-forming set of cardinality at least $t$ — in particular, whether this decision problem is NP-complete on bipartite graphs.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03785v2 (Rafik Sahbi).
solved_when: The computational complexity of computing $SF_2(G)$ on bipartite graphs is determined (equivalently, the complexity of the decision problem above is classified, e.g. shown NP-complete or otherwise resolved).
why: It completes the complexity picture for $SF_2(G)$ on a fundamental graph class, sharpening the boundary between tractable and hard cases of upper $2$-star-forming sets.

title: Zero loci of Bernstein-Sato ideals are not necessarily linear — conjecture linearity
open: Must every Bernstein–Sato ideal of a collection of polynomials have a zero locus that is linear — a finite union of affine subspaces of $\mathbb{C}^r$? Formally, one conjectures that $B_F$ is generated by polynomials of the form $\prod_{j=1}^k (a_{j1}s_1 + \cdots + a_{jr}s_r + a_{j,r+1})$, where $(a_{j1}, \ldots, a_{j,r+1}) \in (\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}^r \setminus \{0\}) \times \mathbb{Q}_{>0}$.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that the zero locus $Z(B_F)$ of any Bernstein–Sato ideal $B_F$ is, or is not, a finite union of affine subspaces of $\mathbb{C}^r$, equivalently that $B_F$ admits generators of the product form above.
why: Linearity of the zero locus would give strong structural control over Bernstein–Sato ideals, which govern jumping coefficients, multiplier ideals, and related invariants in singularity theory; a counterexample would overturn a widely expected structural picture.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04408v1 (Quan Shi, Yongxin Xu, Huaiqing Zuo)

title: Boundary behaviour of stable Allen-Cahn limit-interfaces in Riemannian
open: Can we prove that the level sets converge in the Hausdorff sense even on the boundary? More precisely, can we prove that, assuming $V(\partial) > 0$, for each $b \in (0,1)$ the subsets $\{|u_i| \le 1-b\}$ locally converge in the Hausdorff sense to $\|V\|$ in $\overline{\Omega \setminus U}$ as $i \to \infty$?
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the stated Hausdorff local convergence of the level sets $\{|u_i| \le 1-b\}$ to $\|V\|$ in $\overline{\Omega \setminus U}$ for each $b \in (0,1)$, under the assumption $V(\partial) > 0$.
why: It would extend the boundary behaviour analysis of stable Allen-Cahn limit-interfaces in Riemannian settings to the full Hausdorff sense at the boundary, completing the convergence picture left open by the source paper.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04833v1 (Martin Man-chun Li, Davide Parise, Lorenzo Sarnataro)

title: Gap Amplification for Local Hamiltonians with Combinatorial Soundness
open: Is it possible to recover locality-preserving gap amplification with combinatorial soundness without the use of friendly postselection? In particular, the authors suspect postselection is not essential, and a related goal is to study alphabet reduction in this setting, given that their amplification works only with a large alphabet.
status: Stated as an open problem in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2610.04952v1 (Mitali Bafna, Quynh T. Nguyen, Tina Zhang), where locality-preserving gap amplification with combinatorial soundness is achieved but only with a large alphabet and with the aid of friendly postselection; the authors flag the reliance on postselection as likely the more substantial obstacle and pose recovering their results without it as an interesting open problem, alongside the study of alphabet reduction.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of locality-preserving gap amplification with combinatorial soundness that avoids friendly postselection; progress toward alphabet reduction in this setting would address the natural next step raised in the paper.
why: Removing the postselection dependency would put combinatorial-soundness gap amplification on the same footing as standard amplification techniques, and alphabet reduction is the key step toward making such reductions usable in proof composition.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04952v1 (Mitali Bafna, Quynh T. Nguyen, Tina Zhang)

title: Varieties Admitting Polarized Galois Endomorphisms — conjecture conj: main
open: Let $X$ be an $n$-dimensional Fano manifold of Picard number one. If $X$ admits a non-isomorphic surjective endomorphism, must $X$ be isomorphic to ${P}^n$?
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that every $n$-dimensional Fano manifold of Picard number one admitting a non-isomorphic surjective endomorphism is isomorphic to ${P}^n$.
why: It would complete the classification of Fano manifolds of Picard number one that admit non-isomorphic surjective endomorphisms, a basic case in the study of endomorphisms of varieties.

title: A Proof of the Linear Hadwiger Conjecture — conjecture c:ListHadwiger
open: Does a linear list-coloring analogue of Hadwiger's conjecture hold — that is, is there a positive constant $C$ such that for every integer $t \geq 1$, every graph with no $K_t$ minor is $Ct$-list colorable?
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) of the existence of a positive constant $C$ such that every $K_t$-minor-free graph is $Ct$-list colorable, for every integer $t \geq 1$.
why: It would extend Hadwiger-type coloring guarantees from ordinary coloring to the list-coloring setting, settling how robust the minor–chromatic-number connection is under more constrained color palettes.

title: Presenting a proof of the Kannan-Lovasz-Simonovits conjecture
open: Does there exist a proof of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture of the type suggested — one built on cumulants and stochastic localization for a log-concave probability measure?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2610.05474v1 (Pierre Bizeul, Boaz Klartag, Joseph Lehec).
solved_when: A rigorous proof of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture is given, or a definitive argument shows no such proof of the proposed type can exist.
why: The KLS conjecture is a central open problem in the geometry of log-concave measures; the proposed route via cumulants and stochastic localization would give a new and potentially powerful technique for it.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05474v1 (Pierre Bizeul, Boaz Klartag, Joseph Lehec)

title: Autonomous Quantum Memories from Classical Stochastic Processes
open: Is there a fully autonomous quantum memory — one described by a time-independent, translationally invariant, local Lindbladian — that can be rigorously proven to exist outside the thermal-equilibrium setting, in any geometrical dimension? In other words, can such a memory be constructed and proved to store quantum information reliably in a genuinely autonomous model?
solved_when: A rigorous existence proof (or construction) of a fully autonomous quantum memory — described by a time-independent, translationally invariant, local Lindbladian — outside the thermal-equilibrium setting, in any geometrical dimension, is given.
why: It would establish that reliable quantum information storage does not require thermal-equilibrium assumptions or external time-dependent control, expanding the class of physically realizable self-correcting quantum memories.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05589v1 (Nadav Drechsler, Yuval Oreg, Dorit Aharonov)

title: Autonomous Quantum Memories from Classical Stochastic Processes
open: Can any classical probabilistic cellular automaton (PCA) memory construction be converted, in a black-box manner, into a quantum memory governed by a time-independent Lindbladian? Time-periodic Lindbladians provably need not admit any equivalent time-independent Lindbladian, so the naive route of averaging or "unrolling" the periodic dynamics into a static generator fails, and a genuinely new strengthening of the known theorem is required.
status: Stated as an important open problem in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2610.05589v1 (Nadav Drechsler, Yuval Oreg, Dorit Aharonov). The authors note that examples exist of time-periodic Lindbladians with no effective time-independent Lindbladian yielding equivalent dynamics, so straightforward conversions do not seem to work.
solved_when: A general black-box construction is given that takes an arbitrary PCA-based classical memory as input and outputs a quantum memory generated by a time-independent Lindbladian with equivalent memory-preserving behavior.
why: It would turn classical stochastic self-correction recipes directly into autonomous quantum memories, removing the need for time-dependent (periodic) control, which is hard to implement and analyze in physical quantum memory architectures.
key_works: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05589v1 (Nadav Drechsler, Yuval Oreg, Dorit Aharonov)
